title: Three-dimensional CT evaluation of anatomical constraints during posterior lip drilling in the retrosigmoid approach to the internal auditory canal.
abstract: Purpose To develop a CT-based three-dimensional morphometric framework for evaluating the depth and orientation of posterior lip drilling during the retrosigmoid approach. Methods One hundred normal temporal bones from 50 adults were reconstructed from high-resolution CT. Five surgically relevant landmarks were identified at the endolymphatic sac-duct junction, posterior internal auditory canal (IAC) porus, common crus, lateral IAC fundus, and Bill's bar. Six linear distances and four angular relationships were measured to characterise the drilling corridor relative to the IAC, labyrinth, and endolymphatic sac/duct system. Associations with sex, age, and laterality were explored using a significance threshold of p < 0.01. Results The distance from the posterior IAC porus to the fundus-related landmark was 10.4 ± 1.9 mm, and that from the common crus to the fundus-related landmark was 5.8 ± 1.2 mm. Bill's bar lay 0.9 ± 0.9 mm from the reference plane. The drilling-corridor angle relative to the posterior IAC was 46.1 ± 9.0°. The angle between the endolymphatic sac-common crus axis and the lateral semicircular canal plane was 30.7 ± 15.3° and showed the greatest variability. No significant sex-related or left-right differences were identified. Age showed significant negative correlations with two linear measurements. Conclusion CT-based three-dimensional assessment demonstrated patient-specific variation in drilling orientation as well as depth. This framework may support selective preoperative anatomical planning, but pathological and intraoperative validation is required before these measurements can be considered operative limits.

title: Divergent approaches to rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease: a comparative analysis of international clinical practice guidelines.
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. We compared international and regional clinical practice guidelines to identify agreement, differences, and gaps in RA-ILD care. We conducted a narrative comparative review of five guideline groups: ERS/EULAR, ACR/CHEST, EULAR, PANLAR, and ALAT. Recommendations were assessed across screening, diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment, together with their methodological approaches. Diagnostic recommendations showed the greatest agreement: ILD-focused guidelines emphasized high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT), pulmonary function tests, and multidisciplinary evaluation. Screening recommendations differed: ERS/EULAR and ACR/CHEST favored risk-based assessment, whereas ALAT proposed a broader approach that included lung ultrasound as an adjunct, without replacing HRCT. These differences reflect their scope, methodology, and limited RA-ILD-specific evidence. Prospective comparative studies are needed to inform more consistent care.

title: Latent class analysis of CT-based phenotypes in eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and pulmonary involvement.
abstract: Objectives Pulmonary manifestations of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) are highly heterogeneous, and a standardized CT-based classification is currently lacking. This study aimed to evaluate whether latent class analysis (LCA) of chest CT findings can identify phenotypes with clinical and prognostic relevance in patients with EGPA. Materials and methods We retrospectively enrolled 140 patients with EGPA and pulmonary involvement between 2014 and 2025. Chest CT findings were independently evaluated by two thoracic radiologists and analyzed using LCA to identify CT-based phenotypes. Reproducibility and clinical applicability were assessed by having radiologists reassign patients to phenotypes based on LCA-derived CT patterns while blinded to the original LCA assignments. Baseline characteristics and one-year clinical and radiological outcomes were compared across phenotypes. Modified Poisson regression was used to assess clinical relapse risk. Results LCA identified four distinct phenotypes: bronchial (32.1%; airway-predominant abnormalities), infiltrative (20.7%; parenchyma-predominant abnormalities), mixed (14.3%; combined bronchial and infiltrative features), and nonspecific (32.9%; without a dominant bronchial or infiltrative pattern). The bronchial and infiltrative phenotypes showed more favorable short-term outcomes, whereas the nonspecific phenotype mainly showed stable outcomes. The mixed phenotype remained associated with a higher risk of one-year clinical relapse after adjustment for age, sex, and baseline treatment. Radiologist reassignment showed excellent inter- and intra-observer agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.85 and 0.87). Conclusion LCA enables the identification of CT-based phenotypes with distinct clinical characteristics and short-term outcome patterns in EGPA, suggesting potential prognostic value and a practical role in clinical management. Key points QuestionCan latent class analysis (LCA) of chest CT findings identify imaging phenotypes of pulmonary involvement in eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)? FindingsLCA identified four CT-based phenotypes (bronchial, infiltrative, mixed, and nonspecific), each characterized by distinct clinical and radiological features and short-term outcome patterns. Clinical relevanceCT-based phenotyping may help characterize pulmonary disease heterogeneity in EGPA and identify patients, particularly those with the mixed phenotype, who may require closer monitoring for clinical relapse.

title: Prostate cancer screening with MRI: insights from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group.
abstract: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening for prostate cancer (PCa) remains controversial due to uncertain long-term benefits, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment of indolent disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has transformed the diagnostic pathway of PCa and is increasingly explored as a screening tool. This special report from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group provides an overview of current evidence and insights into the potential role of MRI in PCa screening. MRI-based screening strategies appear to improve detection of clinically significant PCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies and diagnoses of non-significant disease, though long-term outcome data, including mortality impact and interval cancer rates, remain limited. Biparametric MRI is particularly suited for screening due to its shorter acquisition time, reduced operational complexity, and lower costs compared with multiparametric MRI. Two main implementation approaches have emerged: MRI-first pathways, which maximise detection but require substantial resources, and risk-stratified strategies, in which MRI is used after initial assessment (e.g. PSA), potentially offering greater feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Evidence from large trials supports integrating MRI into screening pathways, particularly as a reflex test after PSA screening, although uncertainties remain regarding optimal protocols, interpretation thresholds, follow-up strategies, and long-term outcomes. Key barriers include limited MRI capacity, economic considerations, and the need for standardisation and quality assurance. Advances in artificial intelligence may further enhance efficiency. Overall, MRI has the potential to improve the balance between benefits and harms in PCa screening, but further evidence is required to define its optimal implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can prostate MRI be effectively integrated into population-based prostate cancer screening pathways? Findings MRI-based screening improves detection of csPCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies; biparametric MRI should be the protocol of choice to enhance feasibility, although optimal implementation and long-term outcomes remain uncertain. Clinical relevance MRI may overcome key limitations of PSA-based screening by enhancing the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer while reducing harms such as overdiagnosis and unnecessary biopsies.

title: Imaging-based diagnosis of pancreatic cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of direct comparative studies.
abstract: Objectives Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a fast-evolving malignancy, with resection being the only chance of cure. We aim to determine which imaging technique provides the best diagnostic performance in detecting and assessing the spread of PDAC. Materials and methods Our study was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024567008). On July 9, 2024, a systematic search was conducted in three databases, focusing on direct comparative studies that reported on patients suspected of PDAC who underwent at least two imaging methods. When available, the reference test was represented by pathological examinations, and the diagnostic performance of each diagnostic method was assessed. A bivariate model was used to calculate the pooled sensitivity and specificity, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the meta-analysis. Results Forty direct comparative studies were eligible for meta-analysis. CT, MRI, and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) had no significant differences in diagnostic performance for detecting PDAC. MRI showed higher sensitivity [0.89 [0.67-0.97]) and specificity (0.91 [0.76-0.97]) compared to CT (sensitivity 0.60 (CI: 0.44-0.74) and specificity 0.84 [CI: 0.70-0.93]) in distinguishing liver metastases. CT outperformed MRI for vascular invasion assessment. For lymph node detection, EUS proved to have higher sensitivity than CT or FDG-PET/CT. CT had a higher specificity (0.88 [CI: 0.76-0.94]) compared to MRI (0.63 [CI: 0.48-0.76]) when assessing resectability. Conclusion MRI has a higher pooled sensitivity and specificity for detecting liver metastases of PDAC compared to CT, while the specificity of CT proves to be higher than that of MRI for assessing resectability. Key points QuestionGiven the pancreatic cancer's tight therapeutic window and the need for precise diagnosis, we aim to determine how to best assess it with imaging techniques. FindingsMRI has a significantly higher pooled sensitivity for liver metastases detection than CT. CT has a significantly higher pooled sensitivity for vascular invasion and specificity for resectability assessment than MRI. Clinical relevanceA liver MRI may provide additional value before potentially curative surgery to rule out small metastases. CT should be performed to search for additional metastatic sites and exclude non-resectable cases. Both imaging techniques provide valuable information for assessing pancreatic cancer.

title: Subtraction iodine maps combined with deep learning reconstruction for improved evaluation of bony invasion in temporal bone lesions.
abstract: Objectives To assess the capability of subtraction iodine maps (SIM) combined with deep learning reconstruction (DLR) to evaluate the identification of bone involvement in patients with temporal bone lesions, compared with conventional enhanced CT with hybrid iterative reconstruction (HIR). Materials and methods This prospective study continuously recruited seventy-seven patients (mean age: 46.1 ± 18.9 years; 35 males) with temporal bone lesions who underwent enhanced temporal bone CT scans. Pre-contrast and contrast-enhanced phase images were reconstructed using HIR and DLR. The colored SIM fusion images for evaluation were generated by subtracting the pre-contrast image from the contrast-enhanced image to obtain the SIM, which was then overlaid onto the bone window image. Qualitative scores and quantitative parameters were computed and compared among four groups of images: Enhanced-HIR, Enhanced-DLR, SIM-HIR, and SIM-DLR. Results Quantitative analysis demonstrated that SIM-DLR significantly reduced noise (lower SD values) and increased CNR of the lesion compared to Enhanced-HIR (both p < 0.001). Qualitatively, SIM-DLR exhibited significantly higher scores than conventional Enhanced-HIR in overall image quality, temporal bone lesion detection confidence, lesion contour delineation capability, and temporal bone involvement visualization (all p < 0.001), with high inter-reader agreement (kappa: 0.812-0.904). Enhancement-dependent analysis revealed that SIM showed markedly beneficial scores of lesion detection, contour delineation, and bone involvement visualization in high-enhancement lesions, compared to low-enhancement lesions (all p < 0.05). Conclusion Compared to conventional Enhanced-HIR, SIM-DLR significantly enhanced temporal bone CT imaging by improving image quality, anatomical delineation, and bone involvement visualization, especially for hypervascular lesions. Key points Question Accurately assessing bony invasion by temporal bone lesions is challenging on conventional enhanced CT due to poor lesion-to-bone contrast. Findings SIM combined with DLR improve image quality, lesion delineation, and visualization of bone involvement compared to conventional CT. Clinical relevance This technique enhances preoperative evaluation of temporal bone lesions, particularly hypervascular pathologies, aiding surgical planning and potentially improving treatment precision and outcomes.

title: CT-based pulmonary vascular pruning and emphysema: clinical correlations and prognostic impacts in COPD.
abstract: Objectives Despite evidence of vascular remodeling in emphysematous lungs in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), its natural history and clinical course across phenotypes are not fully understood. We aimed to determine the effect of pruning and emphysema co-occurrence on hemodynamics in the Keio COPD Comorbidity Research (K-CCR) and quality of life (QoL), airflow/diffusion decline, and mortality in the Hokkaido COPD Cohort Study. Materials and methods Pruning was defined as a low blood vessel volume of < 5 mm 2 in the lungs relative to total blood vessel volume (BV5/TBV). Within each cohort, participants were classified into four groups using cohort-specific median dichotomization of BV5/TBV and the percentage of low-attenuation volume. Hemodynamics were assessed using echocardiography-derived estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure (eSPAP). Results Participants from the K-CCR (N = 115) and Hokkaido COPD Cohort Study (N = 96) were evaluated. In the K-CCR, the pruning/severe-emphysema group was associated with poorer QoL and higher eSPAP. In the Hokkaido COPD Cohort Study, the pruning/severe-emphysema group had worse QoL, faster decline in forced expiratory volume in 1 s, and lower carbon monoxide transfer coefficient than the no-pruning/mild-emphysema group. Ten-year survival rates were 80%, 70%, 61%, and 36% for no-pruning/mild-emphysema, no-pruning/severe-emphysema, pruning/mild-emphysema, and pruning/severe-emphysema groups, respectively. In analyses using continuous variables, the percentage of low-attenuation volume was significantly associated with mortality, whereas BV5/TBV was not. Conclusion Pulmonary vascular pruning may be a CT-derived potential biomarker for subtyping patients with poor outcomes, such as impaired hemodynamics and accelerated airflow/diffusion decline, particularly in patients with severe emphysema, requiring further validation. Key points Question Does CT-based pulmonary vascular pruning provide additive prognostic information beyond emphysema severity for predicting pulmonary hemodynamics and longitudinal outcomes in COPD? Findings Categorical analyses suggested that low BV5/TBV was associated with poorer survival, worse hemodynamics, and greater ventilation/diffusion decline in patients with severe emphysema. Clinical relevance CT-derived BV5/TBV may help identify a vascular phenotype associated with worse pulmonary hemodynamics, impaired lung function, reduced quality of life, and adverse long-term outcomes, particularly in patients with severe emphysema, and may contribute to imaging-based phenotyping of COPD.

title: Associations between CT characteristics of lung cancer lesions and histologic subtypes in lung cancer screening.
abstract: Objectives To assess the associations between imaging characteristics and histologic subtype in screen-detected lung cancers. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed histologically confirmed lung cancers from the NELSON trial. Radiological features (location, margins, nodule type, size, volume, volume doubling time (VDT), pleural distance) were annotated using standardized protocols. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, smoking, and stage assessed associations with adenocarcinoma (ADC) versus non-ADC. Sensitivity analyses included models with VDT and were restricted to stage I-II disease. Results Among 213 cancers, 67.5% were ADC and 32.5% non-ADC. Participants were predominantly male (82.4%), with a mean age of 64 years; 73.7% had stage I-II disease. ADCs were more often early stage (86.1% vs 47.8%), smaller (14.6 vs 17.3 mm), and more frequently located in the right upper lobe (49.3% vs 31.9%). In multivariable analysis, larger lesion size was associated with lower odds of ADC (odds ratio (OR) = 0.92, 95% CI 0.85-0.99), while pleural attachment increased the odds (OR = 6.67, 95% CI 1.20-33.33). Compared with the right upper lobe, lesions in the left lower (OR = 0.28), right lower (OR = 0.24), and right middle lobes (OR = 0.17) had lower odds. Model discrimination was acceptable (Area under the curve (AUC) = 0.75), with sensitivity 96% and specificity 29%. In sensitivity analyses, higher VDT was associated with ADC (OR = 5.65), with consistent findings in stage I-II disease. Conclusion In low-dose computed tomography screening, ADCs are smaller, slower-growing, and more often upper-lobe or pleural-based. These patterns may support improved diagnostic interpretation and personalized nodule management. Key points Question Radiological features guide malignancy risk, but their association with histologic subtype in screen-detected lung cancers remains unclear, limiting subtype-specific diagnostic interpretation. Findings Compared to non-adenocarcinomas, adenocarcinomas were smaller, more often pleural-based, and predominantly located in upper lobes, while lower and middle lobe lesions showed lower odds. Clinical relevance Recognizing imaging patterns associated with histologic subtype may improve understanding of tumor biology and inform future multimodal diagnostic approaches.

title: Critical appraisal of artificial intelligence studies for prostate cancer detection on MRI.
abstract: The application of artificial intelligence (AI) to prostate MRI for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection is an active area of medical imaging research. Yet, methodological deficiencies can undermine the reliability and clinical translatability of many published studies. This perspective provides a structured critical appraisal of AI studies in prostate MRI, organised around six evaluation domains: (i) limits of predictability, (ii) reference standard quality, (iii) cohort design and population selection (including spectrum and pathway biases), (iv) benchmark and comparator validity, (v) clinical deployment, and (vi) AI terminology. We illustrate each domain using recently published studies as representative examples, and we ground our perspective in the formal requirements recently established by the PI-RADS Steering Committee for AI development and reporting in biopsy-naive men. Our analysis suggests that apparent near-perfect performance can arise from identifiable and preventable study design choices rather than from technical advancements. Methodological shortcomings may be mistaken for genuine advances; ensuring that the evidence base meets these standards is a prerequisite for population-general utility. KEY POINTS: Question Can the reported near-perfect AI performance for prostate cancer detection on MRI be attributed to study design choices instead of technical advances? Findings Apparent near-perfect diagnostic accuracy can arise from identifiable study design choices, including spectrum bias, pathway bias, imperfect reference standards, and confounded comparisons. Clinical relevance Adopting structured appraisal criteria aligned with PI-RADS Committee requirements helps clinicians distinguish methodologically sound AI tools from those whose reported performance may not generalise to routine clinical populations.

title: Trajectories of pulmonary subsolid nodules in children and adolescents: a retrospective multicenter cohort study.
abstract: Objectives To investigate the clinical course of subsolid nodules (SSNs) in children and adolescents and explore risk factors associated with their progression. Materials and methods This retrospective multicenter cohort investigation enrolled children and adolescents with incidental persistent SSNs between January 2010 and December 2024. The incidence of SSN progression, clinical characteristics, radiologic features, and survival status were assessed. Univariable and multivariable Cox regression analyses were used to identify potential risk factors for nodule growth and subsequent lung cancer diagnosis. Results Overall, 333 incidental persistent SSNs in 241 patients (100 females; median age, 17 years; median follow-up period, 34 months) were included in the final analysis. 35 of the 333 (10.5%) SSNs showed interval growth, including 32 pure ground-glass nodules (PGGNs) and three part-solid nodules (PSNs). 22 PGGNs and two PSNs exhibited an increase in nodule size. One PSN demonstrated an increase in solid components, and ten PGGNs showed a new small solid component. Among 21 surgically resected nodules, approximately 95% (20/21) were early-stage lung adenocarcinoma. There were no deaths or metastases during the follow-up period. PSN was a significant predictor of growth. PSN and ≥ 10 mm were significant predictive risk factors for subsequent lung cancer diagnosis. Conclusion 10.5% of incidental persistent SSNs exhibit subsequent growth. The identified risk factors were predominantly related to varying SSN characteristics. Our findings underscore that the individualized risk-stratified management strategies-long-interval follow-up (2 years or longer) for PGGNs and short-interval follow-up (annual or shorter) for PSNs-should be recommended to guide appropriate clinical decision-making. Key points QuestionDue to the lack of recommendations for SSNs in the pediatric population, clinicians and radiologists might inappropriately apply Fleischner guideline data to these patients. Findings10.5% of persistent SSNs in children and adolescents showed subsequent growth. PSNs are identified as an independent risk factor for predicting nodule growth. Clinical relevanceThe individualized risk-stratified management strategies should be recommended for the pediatric population with SSNs to guide appropriate clinical decision-making.

To investigate the clinical course of subsolid nodules (SSNs) in children and adolescents and explore risk factors associated with their progression.

Materials and methods

This retrospective multicenter cohort investigation enrolled children and adolescents with incidental persistent SSNs between January 2010 and December 2024. The incidence of SSN progression, clinical characteristics, radiologic features, and survival status were assessed. Univariable and multivariable Cox regression analyses were used to identify potential risk factors for nodule growth and subsequent lung cancer diagnosis.

Results

Overall, 333 incidental persistent SSNs in 241 patients (100 females; median age, 17 years; median follow-up period, 34 months) were included in the final analysis. 35 of the 333 (10.5%) SSNs showed interval growth, including 32 pure ground-glass nodules (PGGNs) and three part-solid nodules (PSNs). 22 PGGNs and two PSNs exhibited an increase in nodule size. One PSN demonstrated an increase in solid components, and ten PGGNs showed a new small solid component. Among 21 surgically resected nodules, approximately 95% (20/21) were early-stage lung adenocarcinoma. There were no deaths or metastases during the follow-up period. PSN was a significant predictor of growth. PSN and ≥ 10 mm were significant predictive risk factors for subsequent lung cancer diagnosis.

Conclusion

10.5% of incidental persistent SSNs exhibit subsequent growth. The identified risk factors were predominantly related to varying SSN characteristics. Our findings underscore that the individualized risk-stratified management strategies-long-interval follow-up (2 years or longer) for PGGNs and short-interval follow-up (annual or shorter) for PSNs-should be recommended to guide appropriate clinical decision-making.

Key points

QuestionDue to the lack of recommendations for SSNs in the pediatric population, clinicians and radiologists might inappropriately apply Fleischner guideline data to these patients. Findings10.5% of persistent SSNs in children and adolescents showed subsequent growth. PSNs are identified as an independent risk factor for predicting nodule growth. Clinical relevanceThe individualized risk-stratified management strategies should be recommended for the pediatric population with SSNs to guide appropriate clinical decision-making.

title: Lifting the radiomics performance ceiling: how preprocessing leakage amplifies model multiplicity.
abstract: Objectives To jointly quantify and causally link preprocessing leakage, analytical flexibility and the Rashomon effect in radiomics-based clinical prediction models. Materials and methods Retrospective methodological (specification-curve) analysis of 50 de-identified binary-classification datasets in radMLBench (multicentre; 13 anatomical sites; CT, MRI, PET/CT; median 147 patients per dataset, range 51-969); prediction-model reporting followed CLAIM 2.0 and TRIPOD + AI 2024. We enumerated an analytical multiverse of 456 pipeline specifications (3 scalers × 2 correlation filters × 19 feature selectors × 4 classifiers), each evaluated against the dataset label by 5-fold cross-validation × 10 repetitions. Feature-level preprocessing leakage was assessed by paired global-versus-nested comparison for the synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE), normalisation, correlation filtering and principal component analysis (PCA), pooled by DerSimonian-Laird meta-analysis. Within-subjects causal mediation (43 datasets) tested whether inflation of the best area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) explains leakage-induced Rashomon-set expansion. Results Across the 50 datasets, SMOTE leakage inflated AUC by a pooled 0.09 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.07, 0.11; p < 0.001), exceeding 0.05 in 64%. Pipeline choice shifted AUC by 0.30, classifier dominating (eta-squared = 0.21). At ε = 5%, near-optimal pipelines disagreed on 20-30% of patient classifications (Fleiss kappa = 0.58) and shared < 30% of top features. SMOTE leakage quadrupled the Rashomon set (0.06 to 0.23; p < 0.001); 79% mediated by best-AUC inflation. Radiomics showed 4.8× wider vibration of effects (VoE) but 13× smaller Rashomon ratios than eight tabular benchmarks (both p < 0.001). Conclusion The three sources compound; leakage amplifies model multiplicity by inflating the performance ceiling. Key points Question Whether preprocessing leakage, analytical flexibility and the Rashomon effect jointly compromise the reproducibility of radiomics-based clinical prediction models has not been quantified. Findings Across 50 radiomics datasets, SMOTE leakage inflated AUC by 0.09 and quadrupled the Rashomon set, with 79% causally mediated by best-AUC inflation. Clinical relevance Radiomics-derived clinical prediction models routinely disagree on 20-30% of patients while appearing equally near-optimal. The released three-layer audit tool quantifies this risk per study and should precede any clinical deployment claim.

title: UroVision: a new artificial intelligence software for functional magnetic resonance urography evaluation in children with congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract.
abstract: Objectives This study compared UroVision, a novel AI-based tool for automated three-dimensional (3D) segmentation and magnetic resonance urography (MRU) functional analysis, with the validated ImageJ MRU software, focusing on split renal function (SRF) and drainage curve classification in children with congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT). Materials and methods MRU examinations in children with CAKUT were retrospectively analysed using UroVision and ImageJ MRU. UroVision functional assessment was limited to the two-dimensional slice showing the largest amount of renal parenchyma, matching the ImageJ MRU workflow. Two paediatric radiologists independently performed the evaluations. Agreement was assessed using Pearson correlation, linear regression, Bland-Altman analysis, and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Drainage curve morphology was evaluated by an expert pediatric radiologist, with inter-method agreement assessed using weighted Cohen's κ. The full 3D UroVision analysis was reviewed to aid the interpretation of borderline and discordant cases. Results Fifty patients (28 males, 22 females; mean age 2.4 years, range 0-18 years) were included, yielding 100 kidneys for validation. UroVision showed excellent agreement with ImageJ MRU: renal volume correlation was high (r = 0.99), while functional parameters showed moderate correlation (glomerular slope r = 0.63; Patlak coefficient r = 0.57). Bland-Altman analysis showed minimal bias. Inter-reader and intra-reader reproducibility were excellent (ICCs: 0.87-1.00 and 0.89-0.99, respectively). Agreement for drainage curves was similarly high (weighted κ = 0.86). Full 3D analysis enabled reclassification of borderline curves in 16 out of 23 kidneys. Conclusions UroVision provides results comparable to ImageJ MRU, while offering automated analyses and improved reproducibility. Key points Question Can UroVision provide reliable quantitative and qualitative renal and urinary tract functional assessment in children with CAKUT compared with ImageJ MRU? Findings UroVision showed excellent agreement with ImageJ MRU for renal function parameters and drainage curve classification, with high inter- and intra-reader reproducibility. Clinical relevance UroVision uses AI-based automated MRU analysis to deliver reproducible and standardised functional assessment in children with CAKUT, reducing operator dependence and improving workflow efficiency while providing reproducible and standardised functional assessment in clinical practice.

title: Restaging the primary tumor in localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma after systemic therapy: a scoping review of the role of CT, FDG-PET, and CA19-9.
abstract: Objectives The introduction of improved multi-agent systemic therapies has made restaging and treatment response assessment in patients with localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) increasingly complex. This scoping review aims to assess and compare methods for local disease restaging and treatment response assessment in localized PDAC, with a focus on their association with resectability, overall survival (OS), and R0-resection rates. Materials and methods This scoping review included studies on restaging in patients with PDAC following systemic therapy using CT and PET/CT from MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL. Results Among 4680 identified studies, 20 fulfilled the eligibility criteria. Most (n = 15) studies analyzed CT, and 5 analyzed PET/CT. Groups of restaging methods included new response categories, size-based metrics, volume, vascular contact, tumor attenuation, fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) PET/CT derived metabolic parameters, and resectability criteria. Dual-energy CT-derived extracellular volume (DECT-ECV) was evaluated as a baseline predictive biomarker. Associations between restaging methods and outcomes were reported inconsistently: some studies found significant associations for specific methods, whereas others did not. No restaging method showed a consistent association with both R0-resection and survival across all studies. Conclusion Restaging of localized PDAC after systemic treatment remains challenging due to the limited accuracy of RECIST 1.1, particularly for the classifications partial response and stable disease. The current evidence suggests that integrating additional imaging features, alternative imaging modalities, and the biomarker carbohydrate antigen (CA)19-9 may improve the assessment of resectability and prognosis. These findings support a future version of RECIST 1.1 to alert clinicians to this issue. Key points Question How effective are current (PET/)CT-based restaging methods in assessing local disease resectability and prognosis in localized PDAC after modern multi-agent systemic therapy? Findings Current restaging methods show inconsistent association with R0-resection and survival; RECIST 1.1 is particularly limited for the assessment of partial response and stable disease. Clinical relevance Current evidence confirms a need to integrate additional imaging features and the biomarker CA19-9, during restaging in patients with localized pancreatic cancer after modern systemic therapy to improve accuracy and reduce the risk of missed treatment options.

title: Segmentation-based morphometric analysis of neck abscesses on MRI: associations with disease severity.
abstract: Objectives Abscess diameter on MRI is an established predictor of clinical severity in neck infections, but this single measurement does not characterize three-dimensional morphology. This study evaluated whether segmentation-derived volume, sphericity, and compactness provide incremental prognostic value beyond conventional diameter. Materials and methods In 227 consecutive patients with surgically confirmed neck abscesses, abscess masks were segmented on post-contrast T1-weighted MRI. Three morphometric features were extracted: volume, sphericity, and compactness; their associations with intensive care unit (ICU) admission and a prolonged hospital stay (exceeding 5 days) were evaluated using multivariable models. Results Of 227 patients, 33 (15%) required ICU admission, and 40 (18%) had a prolonged hospital stay. Sphericity was lower in ICU patients (median 0.35 vs. 0.45, p = 6.6 × 10 - 5 ) and in those with prolonged stay (p = 9.1 × 10 - 6 ). In multivariable models, volume improved upon manual diameter for ICU prediction (area under the curve 0.841 [95% CI 0.78-0.90] vs. 0.816 [0.74-0.88]); adding sphericity improved prolonged stay prediction (R 2 0.246 vs. 0.216, p = 0.005). Interobserver agreement was excellent (ICC 0.97-0.99). Conclusion Segmentation-derived abscess volume, sphericity, and compactness provide complementary prognostic information beyond conventional diameter measurement for assessing neck infection severity. Key points Question Can segmentation-derived morphometric features of neck abscesses (volume, sphericity, compactness) improve prognostication of ICU admission and prolonged hospital stay beyond conventional diameter measurement on MRI? Findings Abscess volume outperformed manual diameter for predicting ICU admissions, and lower sphericity independently predicted prolonged hospital stay beyond abscess size in multivariable models. Clinical relevance Segmentation-derived morphometric features offer reproducible, quantitative tools for stratifying neck abscess severity in surgically managed patients; their value for guiding individual treatment decisions was not directly evaluated and warrants prospective validation.

title: VERIDAH: solving enumeration anomaly-aware vertebra labeling across imaging sequences.
abstract: Objectives Although the identification of enumeration anomalies has potential clinical implications for chronic back pain and operation planning, the thoracolumbar junction is poorly assessed and rarely described in clinical reports. Additionally, even though multiple deep-learning-based vertebra labeling algorithms exist, there is a lack of methods to automatically label enumeration anomalies. Materials and methods We introduce "Vertebra Identification with Anomaly Handling" (VERIDAH), a novel vertebra labeling algorithm based on multiple classification heads combined with a weighted vertebra sequence prediction algorithm. We use the NAKO dataset for MRI and a CT cohort to retrospectively evaluate the labeling performance by computing how often the model is correct in predicting the vertebra labels, including enumeration anomalies. Statistical significance was assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results On 1000 T2w sagittal (mean age 52 ± 11, 52% female) and 365 CT (mean age 74 ± 21, 44% female) images, we show that our approach surpasses existing models on T2w TSE sagittal (98.30% vs. 94.24% of subjects with all vertebrae correctly labeled, p < 0.01) and CT imaging (99.18% vs. 77.26% of subjects with all vertebrae correctly labeled, p < 0.01) and works in arbitrary field-of-view images. title: The role of cardiac CT with late iodine enhancement in patients with acute cardiac symptoms and troponin elevation in the era of high-sensitivity assays.
abstract: Objectives Diagnostic workup of patients with acute cardiac symptoms, troponin elevation, and no acute myocardial infarction (AMI) criteria is challenging. Cardiac CT angiography (CCTA) rules out obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Adding late iodine enhancement and extracellular volume fraction (CCTA + LIE/ECV) provides insights into myocardial injury. However, the impact on working diagnosis, agreement with discharge diagnosis, and mid-term safety of implementing CCTA + LIE/ECV in the emergency department remains uncertain. Materials and methods Prospective study on consecutive patients presenting, from June 2018 to February 2025, with acute chest pain or equivalents, elevated troponin, and no AMI diagnosis, excluding previously revascularized patients. Patients underwent CCTA to rule out obstructive CAD (≥ 50% stenosis). CCTA-negative patients underwent myocardial tissue characterization with LIE; if negative, ECV was quantified. Primary endpoint modification of working diagnosis by CT. Secondary endpoints: agreement between CT and discharge diagnoses after standard-of-care assessment; mid-term major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) in CT-negative patients. Results Among 191 patients (age 70 [55-79] years; 53% men), CCTA identified obstructive CAD in 76/191 (40%). LIE/ECV were positive in 58/106 (55%) of CCTA-negative cases, revealing myocarditis in 32/106 (30%), AMI with non-obstructive CAD in 8/106 (8%), Takotsubo in 14/106 (13%), amyloidosis in 3/106 (3%), and dilated cardiomyopathy in 1/106 (1%). CT modified the working diagnosis in 91/191 (48%) patients. Agreement between CT and discharge diagnosis was 0.94 (95% CI 0.89-0.97). In patients with negative CCTA + LIE/ECV, no MACEs occurred after 24 [interquartile range, 19-29] months. Conclusion In patients with acute symptoms, elevated troponin, and no AMI, a protocol combining CCTA + LIE/ECV enables etiologic assessment of coronary and myocardial conditions, refines working diagnosis, and entails a favorable prognosis when negative. Key points Question Patients with acute cardiac symptoms, troponin elevation, and no evidence of acute myocardial infarction represent a diagnostic challenge: cardiac CT with late iodine enhancement may have diagnostic and prognostic implications. Findings CT angiography with late iodine enhancement provided a diagnosis in 75% of patients and modified the working diagnosis in 48%. In the 25% CT-negative patients, no adverse events occurred at mid-term follow-up. Clinical relevance A CT protocol including coronary artery evaluation and myocardial tissue characterization may provide a rapid etiological diagnosis in patients with acute symptoms and troponin elevation, potentially supporting earlier clinical decision-making and reducing the need for additional downstream testing.

title: From dusk till dawn?-Night shift-induced fatigue, diagnostic performance, and AI assistance in chest radiography.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the impact of night shift-induced fatigue on radiology residents' diagnostic performance and to assess whether AI assistance offsets potential performance loss. Materials and methods In this prospective intra-individual reader study, ten radiology residents (mean experience: 35 months; three women) interpreted three sets of 33 chest radiographs before and after a first-call on-site night shift. Sessions included two pre-shift readings (morning/afternoon, without AI) and two post-shift readings (morning, with/without AI). Eye tracking captured fixation duration and saccade count, and fatigue was defined as a ≥ 5% reduction in the slope of the saccadic main sequence between pre- and post-shift sessions. Diagnostic accuracy (Cohen's κ vs. expert majority vote), efficiency (mean reporting time per radiograph), eye-tracking metrics, and user surveys were analyzed with generalized linear mixed models and post-hoc Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Results Six of ten radiology residents were classified as fatigued, among whom diagnostic accuracy declined significantly post-shift (from κ = 0.71 ± 0.05 to κ = 0.61 ± 0.10; p < 0.001), with reduced fixation duration (p = 0.010) and saccade count (p = 0.015). Non-fatigued readers showed a smaller decline in accuracy (from κ = 0.72 ± 0.03 to κ = 0.65 ± 0.03; p = 0.037). Reporting times remained stable pre- and post-shift (p ≥ 0.463). AI assistance did not significantly improve diagnostic accuracy (Δκ = 0.03-0.04; p ≥ 0.525). Reporting times were numerically shorter with AI assistance in fatigued readers (Δ6.3 s; p = 0.122) and significantly shorter in non-fatigued readers (Δ9.9 s; p = 0.031). Surveys indicated mental exhaustion and reduced focus in fatigued readers. Conclusion Night-shift-induced fatigue impaired diagnostic accuracy without slowing reporting speed, raising patient safety concerns. The utilized AI model did not restore pre-shift performance. Key points Question Night-shift-induced fatigue may reduce diagnostic accuracy of radiology residents in chest radiography, yet its objective quantification and the compensatory potential of AI assistance remain unclear. Findings Fatigue, based on eye-tracking measurements of oculomotor efficiency, reduced diagnostic accuracy after night shifts without slowing reporting speed; AI assistance did not significantly improve accuracy. Clinical relevance Night-shift-induced fatigue can lower diagnostic accuracy in chest radiography despite unchanged reporting speed, posing patient-safety risks. The AI model used in this study cannot fully compensate for fatigue-related performance decline.

title: Low-dose vs standard-dose photon-counting CT for myopathy-associated interstitial lung disease: a prospective feasibility study.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the clinical utility of photon counting computed tomography (PCCT)-derived quantitative parameters for assessing interstitial lung disease (ILD) burden in patients with inflammatory idiopathic myopathy (IIM), comparing standard-dose (SD) and tin-filtered low-dose (LD) protocols, and to assess the added value of ultrathin reconstructions. Materials and methods In this single-centre prospective study (September 2023-November 2024), outpatients with IIM-ILD underwent two consecutive PCCT scans. Quantitative ILD features were extracted using a commercial deep-learning software (ContextFlow ADVANCE Chest CT). Primary analyses compared LD 1.0 mm with SD 1.0 mm reconstructions using Bland-Altman analysis, with exploratory analyses of ultrathin (0.4 mm) reconstructions. Correlation analyses between deep learning-derived quantitative parameters, visual assessment, and pulmonary function tests were performed. Results Forty-eight adults with IIM-ILD (40 females; mean age, 53.88 ± 11.13 years) were included. The LD protocol achieved a substantial dose reduction (CTDIvol: 0.77 vs 5.40 mGy) while maintaining good agreement with SD (mean net differences [MNDs] < 1% for all patterns). LD-1.0 mm protocol yielded higher volume of ground-glass opacity (MND, 0.98%) and lower volume of fibrosis extent (MND, -0.64%). Reticular pattern showed strong association with FVC% (rho SD1.0mm = -0.62, p < 0.001) and DLCO% (rho SD1.0mm = -0.73, p < 0.001), with similar correlations observed under LD acquisition (Δrho ≤ 0.02). Ultrathin reconstructions yielded greater measurement of bronchiectasis (MND, 0.13% on SD scans). Conclusion LD PCCT serves as a radiation-sparing alternative for quantitative disease assessment. Ultrathin reconstructions provide limited additional value. Future longitudinal studies are warranted to validate the performance of LD PCCT for disease monitoring. Key points Question Can LD photon-counting CT provide robust quantitative assessment of ILD burden in patients with inflammatory myopathy compared with SD imaging? Findings Deep learning segmentation yielded LD ILD patterns that closely matched SD results, with all MNDs below 1%. Clinical relevance LD PCCT maintains quantitative robustness and physiological validity for IIM-ILD assessment, with total disease burden showing good agreement with the SD protocol, offering a radiation-sparing alternative without compromising CT-physiology correlation.

title: CT features of extra-pancreatic nerve plexus invasion predict mortality in early-stage pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Objective The presence of extra-pancreatic nerve plexus invasion (EPNI) in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is known to correlate with aggressive disease, however, it is unknown whether specific pathways or morphologies carry different prognostic implications. This study evaluates whether distinct CT-defined patterns of EPNI predict mortality in PDAC. Materials and methods This retrospective, single-center study included 89 patients with pathologically confirmed PDAC who underwent preoperative pancreatic protocol multidetector CT (MDCT) followed by surgical resection. Patients were identified from an institutional database and required available preoperative CT and histopathology. Two blinded, experienced radiologists reviewed MDCT images to assess EPNI, which was categorized by anatomic pathway and morphologic pattern. Overall survival was compared between EPNI-positive and EPNI-negative groups and among EPNI subtypes using log-rank testing, with stratification by tumor stage. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, and surgical margin were performed. Results A total of 89 patients (M/F: 54/35), median age: 66 years (IQR, 60-70 years), were evaluated. CT evidence of EPNI was present in 65 patients (73%) and was associated with decreased overall survival (p < 0.001). This association remained significant in Stage I tumors (p < 0.001). PPC2 pathway involvement (p < 0.001) and mass-with-stranding morphology (p < 0.001) were each associated with reduced overall survival. PPC2 (p = 0.003) and mass-with-stranding (p < 0.001) remained significant in stage I tumors. Conclusion Preoperative CT detection of EPNI, especially PPC2 pathway involvement and mass-with-stranding morphology, identifies high-risk PDAC patients. Key points Question Extra pancreatic nerve plexus invasion in pancreatic adenocarcinoma is associated with aggressive disease, but the prognostic significance of specific pathways or morphologies remains unknown. Findings Plexus pancreaticus capitalis 2 involvement and mass-with-stranding morphology in EPNI of pancreatic adenocarcinoma are associated with decreased overall survival. Clinical relevance Identifying high-risk EPNI features on CT may facilitate early prognostic stratification and inform surgical and neoadjuvant treatment planning in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

title: Partial vs. whole-gland salvage hifu after radiotherapy failure: oncological and functional outcomes.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the long-term oncological and functional outcomes of whole-gland and partial-gland salvage high-intensity focused ultrasound (S-HIFU) in patients with radiorecurrent prostate cancer, for whom local recurrence after radiotherapy remains a major therapeutic challenge and radical salvage surgery is associated with substantial morbidity. Methods We performed a retrospective single-center study including 138 patients treated with S-HIFU between August 2006 and October 2023 for biopsy-proven local recurrence without metastatic disease. Treatments consisted of whole-gland or partial-gland ablation, including hemi-gland and focal therapy. Oncological outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analyses and multivariable Cox regression models evaluating progression-free survival (PFS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), and cancer-specific survival (CSS). Postoperative complications were graded according to the Clavien-Dindo classification. Results After a median follow-up of over five years, 5-year PFS, MFS, and CSS rates were 43.6%, 85%, and 95%, respectively. Higher pre-HIFU prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels and ISUP grade ≥ 5 independently predicted disease progression. No significant differences in PFS or MFS were observed between whole-gland and partial-gland treatments. Acute urinary retention occurred in 33% of patients and voiding dysfunction in 39.9%, requiring surgical management in 34.1% of cases. Severe complications were significantly more frequent after whole-gland compared with partial-gland S-HIFU (48.3% vs. 29.8%, p < 0.05). Conclusion S-HIFU represents a viable salvage option after radiotherapy failure. Our results support that partial-gland S-HIFU significantly reduces severe morbidity while maintaining comparable oncological outcomes compared to whole-gland S-HIFU in appropriately selected patients.

title: Impact of magnetic resonance imaging-based diagnostic pathway on oncologic outcomes of localised prostate cancer between primary treatment modalities: a Will-Rogers phenomenon?
abstract: Background The MRI pathway (pre-biopsy MRI-targeted plus saturation biopsies, MRI-Bx) outperforms transrectal ultrasound systematic prostate biopsy (TRUS-Bx) in diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). However, there is a dearth of data on how this paradigm shift influences biochemical recurrence (BCR)-free survival in patients after radical prostatectomy (RP) or radiotherapy (RT). We aim to evaluate BCR-free survival in the MRI-Bx era stratified by primary treatment modalities in a large contemporary cohort. Methods We retrospectively reviewed localised prostate cancer patients diagnosed by MRI-Bx or TRUS-Bx and treated with RP or RT between 2010 and 2021. Patients diagnosed and staged by PSMA-PET were excluded. BCR was defined as two successive prostatic specific antigen (PSA) > 0.2 ng/mL after RP or a rise of 2 ng/mL from PSA nadir after RT within 3 years. Kaplan-Meier (KM) analyses and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression were performed for BCR-free survival. Results A total of 1674 men included (1061 RP, 613 RT; 1075 TRUS-Bx, 599 MRI-Bx; median follow-up 38 months). Across all risk group, MRI-Bx yielded higher BCR-free survival at all timepoints in RP patients, especially in high-risk disease (3-year: 85% vs. 71%). In RT patients, MRI-Bx yielded no significant difference across all timepoints. On multivariable regression, MRI-Bx approach independently predicted BCR in RP patients (hazard ratio (HR) 0.60, 95% CI 0.40-0.90, p = 0.013) but not in RT patients (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.31-3.85, p = 0.945) after adjusting for age, PSA, clinical T stage, Gleason grade group, adjuvant ADT and EAU risk groups. In terms of GG concordance after RP, MRI-Bx demonstrated decreased GG upgrading than TRUS-Bx group (23.1% vs. 27.4%) but increased GG downgrading (20.6% vs. 14.4%), which was statistically significant (p = 0.025). Conclusions Patients managed via the MRI pathway exhibited improved BCR-free survival following RP, reflecting a risk migration consistent with the Will-Rogers phenomenon. This survival advantage was attenuated in the RT cohort, potentially due to difference in BCR definition and adjuvant ADT use. The risk reclassification in the RP cohort after MRI pathway adoption underscores the necessity of new risk models integrating quantitative MRI parameters to better select patients for surgery. Longer follow-up is required to determine the impact on overall and cancer-specific survival.

title: [Stargardt disease (ABCA4-asssociated retinopathy): Overview of clinical aspects, classification and differential diagnoses].
abstract: Morbus Stargardt (STGD1) is the most common autosomal recessive macular dystrophy and is caused by biallelic variants in the ABCA4 gene located on chromosome 1. More than 1200 disease-associated variants have been described, causing a broad phenotypic spectrum. The hallmark feature is a bilateral, typically slowly progressive visual impairment, although best-corrected visual acuity can be preserved for a long time in patients with foveal sparing. The disease is characterized by lipofuscin accumulation in the retinal pigment epithelium, manifesting as fundus flavimaculatus on funduscopic examination, outer retinal atrophy on optical coherence tomography (OCT) and a characteristic pattern on fundus autofluorescence imaging. While earlier classifications were primarily based on clinical and electrophysiological criteria, current approaches increasingly focus on genotype-phenotype correlations, which can also enable prognostic statements. Severe, early-onset disease courses are predominantly associated with loss of function variants, whereas certain genotypes have been linked to milder and later-onset manifestations. The differential diagnosis remains challenging due to considerable phenotypic overlap with other autosomal-dominant and autosomal-recessive macular dystrophies. Moreover, particularly in late-onset cases, differentiation from geographic atrophy secondary to age-related macular degeneration can be necessary.

title: Atypical presacral masses in Currarino syndrome: a case series.
abstract: Introduction Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. While anterior meningoceles and teratomas are the most commonly reported lesions, an expanding body of literature suggests a broader spectrum of presacral pathology. We present three cases from our institution that expand the phenotypic range of presacral masses associated with Currarino syndrome, including lesions not previously well described in this population. Case presentation Three cases are presented. Final pathologic diagnoses included myxopapillary ependymoma, mature cystic teratoma, and neuroendocrine tumor arising within a teratoma. Conclusion These cases highlight the considerable heterogeneity of presacral lesions in Currarino syndrome and identify two underrecognized or previously unreported tumor types: myxopapillary ependymoma and neuroendocrine tumor. Surgical management must be individualized and often requires a multidisciplinary approach. Future studies will further clarify genotype-phenotype relationships and improve diagnostic and management strategies in this complex syndrome. Established facts Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. Presacral masses are most commonly anterior meningoceles and teratomas. A wider spectrum of lesions has been reported, underscoring the complexity of the syndrome and the importance of thorough evaluation and management of presacral pathology. Novel insights In Case 1, we report a previously undescribed association of myxopapillary ependymoma with a retrorectal teratoma in the setting of Currarino syndrome. Case 2 illustrates the potential for significant enlargement of presacral meningoceles with associated teratomas with a rare instance of prenatal diagnosis by ultrasound. Case 3 expands the spectrum of presacral pathology in Currarino syndrome by demonstrating a neuroendocrine tumor.

Introduction

Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. While anterior meningoceles and teratomas are the most commonly reported lesions, an expanding body of literature suggests a broader spectrum of presacral pathology. We present three cases from our institution that expand the phenotypic range of presacral masses associated with Currarino syndrome, including lesions not previously well described in this population.

Case presentation

Three cases are presented. Final pathologic diagnoses included myxopapillary ependymoma, mature cystic teratoma, and neuroendocrine tumor arising within a teratoma.

Conclusion

These cases highlight the considerable heterogeneity of presacral lesions in Currarino syndrome and identify two underrecognized or previously unreported tumor types: myxopapillary ependymoma and neuroendocrine tumor. Surgical management must be individualized and often requires a multidisciplinary approach. Future studies will further clarify genotype-phenotype relationships and improve diagnostic and management strategies in this complex syndrome.

Established facts

Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. Presacral masses are most commonly anterior meningoceles and teratomas. A wider spectrum of lesions has been reported, underscoring the complexity of the syndrome and the importance of thorough evaluation and management of presacral pathology.

Novel insights

In Case 1, we report a previously undescribed association of myxopapillary ependymoma with a retrorectal teratoma in the setting of Currarino syndrome. Case 2 illustrates the potential for significant enlargement of presacral meningoceles with associated teratomas with a rare instance of prenatal diagnosis by ultrasound. Case 3 expands the spectrum of presacral pathology in Currarino syndrome by demonstrating a neuroendocrine tumor.

title: Addressing unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis using endoscopic suturectomy and barrel-stave osteotomies: surgical technique and literature review.
abstract: Purpose Unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis (ULC) is a rare cranial deformity requiring intervention to correct asymmetry of the posterior skull. Conventional open remodeling and distraction osteogenesis offer robust expansion but carry risks of higher blood loss, hardware complications, or reoperation. We report a novel, minimally invasive technique combining endoscopic lambdoid suturectomy with barrel-stave osteotomies, supplemented by a literature review. Case description A 2-month-old healthy male presented with classic left ULC features, including occipitoparietal flattening, ipsilateral mastoid bulge, contralateral parietal bulge, and ear level asymmetry, confirmed by 3D computed tomography. Under endoscopic guidance through two small incisions, a 10-cm-long by 1.2-cm-wide lambdoid suturectomy was performed. To enhance immediate intraoperative expansion, seven 3-cm barrel-stave osteotomies were placed perpendicularly along the superior (4 cuts) and inferior (3 cuts) suture margins and gently greenstick-fractured outward. The estimated blood loss was 10 mL without perioperative complications. Postoperative cranial molding helmet therapy was initiated on day 10. At the 4-month follow-up visit, 3D surface scanning demonstrated marked improvement in head shape and symmetry. Conclusions Our method, endoscopic suturectomy and barrel-stave osteotomies on a single patient with unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis, demonstrated safe and favorable outcomes. We believe the addition of barrel-stave osteotomies to suturectomy may yield superior clinical outcomes, compared to conventional endoscopic-assisted procedures with suturectomy alone. However, it is necessary to accumulate a larger number of cases and conduct long-term follow-up studies to further validate this hypothesis.

title: Anatomical and clinical characteristics of pediatric endoscopic third ventriculostomy performed with a small-diameter neuroendoscope.
abstract: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) is an established treatment for selected pediatric patients with obstructive hydrocephalus. Although the foramen of Monro constitutes the principal anatomical corridor to the third ventricle, its preoperative radiological characterization has been scarcely investigated. This study aimed to describe the radiological characteristics of the foramen of Monro in a consecutive pediatric ETV cohort treated with a small-diameter rigid neuroendoscope and to explore its relationship with ventricular morphology and clinical outcome. A retrospective observational study was performed including the complete consecutive series of 17 pediatric patients who underwent ETV at our institution between March 2022 and November 2024. All procedures were performed using the PaediScope® neuroendoscope. The radiological diameter of the right foramen of Monro was measured on axial T2-weighted MRI together with the Evans Index and third ventricular diameter. Clinical, radiological, and operative variables were retrospectively collected. Correlations between radiological parameters and clinical outcome were analyzed using non-parametric statistical methods. The mean radiological diameter of the right foramen of Monro was 2.79 ± 0.81 mm. Moderate positive correlations were observed between the foramen of Monro diameter and the preoperative Evans Index (ρ = 0.588, p = 0.013), preoperative third ventricular diameter (ρ = 0.606, p = 0.010), and postoperative third ventricular diameter (ρ = 0.568, p = 0.017). No significant association was found between the radiological diameter of the foramen of Monro and the subsequent requirement for definitive ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement or postoperative ventricular reduction. Three patients (17.6%) required definitive ventriculoperitoneal shunting during the available clinical follow-up. These patients had significantly lower Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy Success Scores than patients who maintained ETV function (p = 0.016). Intraoperative visualization was good in 16/17 procedures and moderate in one, and no major intraoperative complications were recorded. The radiological measurement of the foramen of Monro correlated with ventricular morphology but was not associated with clinical outcome after pediatric ETV. Rather than representing the true anatomical diameter of the surgical corridor, this measurement should be interpreted as a standardized radiological descriptor of ventricular anatomy. The small diameter neuroendoscope was technically applicable across the range of ventricular anatomy represented in this complete consecutive cohort, although the absence of a comparator precludes conclusions regarding device-specific benefit. The study demonstrates the feasibility of obtaining this measurement from routine preoperative MRI and provides preliminary anatomical data that may support future prospective studies evaluating technical planning for pediatric ventricular endoscopy.

title: Validation of PECARN as a clinical decision rule for CT imaging of children with blunt abdominal trauma: a single centre retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Background Blunt traumatic injuries are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in children. Contrast enhanced computed tomography (CT) is the best imaging tool for screening patients at risk of blunt abdominal injury. Concerns existed on potential overuse and the radiation risks. We aim at evaluating paediatric use of trauma CT scan. Methods Children with traumatic injuries who attended a tertiary trauma centre from January 2000 to December 2024 were included to evaluate the use of trauma CT scan and patterns of paediatric abdominal trauma. We excluded those with penetrating or isolated head injury. The Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) algorithm was applied retrospectively with the aim of validating the use of PECARN. Results Total of 1138 paediatic trauma admissions were identified during the study period and 70% (n 802) had blunt trauma. 483 patients were included after excluding patients with isolated head injury and missing data. 90 days trauma related mortality was 0.7% with one patient died within 24 hours of admission. Overall Injury Severity Score (ISS) was 3.52±5.95 which appeared to increase with age (rho 0.289, p <0.01).111 patients received CT scan, among which 35 are whole body CT. Significant findings were detected in 30% of these scans, 25 required intervention. Patients with higher trauma index and lower GCS, trauma call activation, older aged at presentation were more likely to receive a scan (p<0.001). No pathology was missed in the no CT group. PECARN validation was performed on 200 patients, There were no missed scans and pathologies in PECARN negative patients. Sensitivity was 100%, specificity was 96.5%, negative predictive value was 100%. Conclusion A significant portion of children had negative trauma CT scan and did not need intervention. Use of clinical decision rule is warranted in identifying children at lower risk to minimize unnecessary imaging.

title: Routine pulmonary wound closure after thoracoscopic sublobar resection for congenital lung malformations in children: impact on early recovery, one-year CT-based lung expansion, and the learning curve.
abstract: Background The necessity of routine pulmonary parenchymal wound closure following thoracoscopic sublobar resection for congenital lung malformations (CLMs) in children remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the association of routine wound closure with drainage-related recovery, perioperative outcomes, one-year computed tomography (CT)-based lung re-expansion, and the procedural learning curve. Methods Consecutive children who underwent thoracoscopic sublobar resection for CLMs between January 2021 and March 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. The cohort was divided into a non-closure group and a routine-closure group according to wound management strategy. Pulmonary wound closure was performed using an absorbable barbed suture, generally proceeding from the peripheral or lower-tension side toward the central or higher-tension region. Irregular wounds were managed by initiating closure from multiple peripheral points converging centrally while preserving the natural axis of residual bronchi and vasculature. Outcomes included chest tube duration, drainage volume, prolonged air leak, chest tube reinsertion, postoperative hospital stay, perioperative complications, one-year CT-based volumetric indices, and closure-time learning curve metrics. Results A total of 285 children were included, comprising 75 in the non-closure group and 210 in the closure group. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. Compared with the non-closure group, the closure group exhibited significantly shorter chest tube duration (0.87 ± 0.74 vs. 2.81 ± 1.99 days, P < 0.001), lower postoperative drainage volume (2.12 ± 0.70 vs. 7.21 ± 2.58 mL/kg/day, P < 0.001), reduced rates of prolonged air leak and drainage failure, and shorter postoperative hospital stay (5.63 ± 0.83 vs. 7.68 ± 2.10 days, P < 0.001). At one-year follow-up, CT-based volumetric assessment revealed no evidence that wound closure restricted residual lung re-expansion. Closure time decreased from approximately 22 min in the early phase to 11 min in the late phase, with learning curve inflection points identified at cases 47 and 135. Conclusions Routine pulmonary wound closure following thoracoscopic sublobar resection for pediatric CLMs was associated with improved drainage-related recovery and shorter hospitalization, without compromising one-year lung re-expansion on CT. Although closure adds a procedural step, efficiency improved substantially with experience, demonstrating a quantifiable learning curve.

title: Effectiveness of prenatal predictors for congenital diaphragmatic hernia on survival to discharge and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation requirement: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Introduction Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is associated with high mortality and morbidity. Antenatal counselling enables parents to prepare for the postnatal outcomes and relies on effective prognostic tools. Ultrasound (USS) predictors including observed/expected lung head ratio (o/e LHR) and liver position, are used independently, or combined into severity classifications. The aim was to evaluate the association between USS predictors, and severity classifications with survival to discharge and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) requirement in prenatally diagnosed CDH at Birmingham Women's and Children's Hospital (BWC). Methods CDH patients from BWC with dates of birth between 1st December 2013-1st December 2023 were retrospectively collected. Study inclusion required o/e LHR measurement between 22- and 32-weeks gestational age (GA.) Comparisons between groups was assessed by Fisher exact test and Mann-Whitney U test. Logistic regression was performed to determine prognostic ability, with area under curve (AUC) calculated. Results 91 eligible patients were identified, which included 82 left-sided, and 9 right-sided CDH. Overall, 55% survived to discharge and 13% required ECMO. In the left CDH cohort, 57% of infants survived to discharge, and 15% required ECMO. O/e LHR, liver position and the combined predictive model including o/e LHR and liver position were predictive of survival to discharge with good prognostic ability (AUC 0.769, AUC 0.703, and AUC 0.823, respectively). O/e LHR, liver position, and the combined predictive model were not predictive of ECMO requirement. In the right CDH patients, 33% survived to discharge, O/e LHR and liver position were not predictive of survival to discharge. Conclusion O/e LHR, liver position and the combination of these predictors, predicted survival to discharge in prenatally diagnosed left CDH with the combined model, the most predictive particularly in the isolated left CDH sub-group. Further analysis into effective predictors for ECMO requirement, and for right and complex left CDH is required.

O/e LHR, liver position and the combined predictive model including o/e LHR and liver position were predictive of survival to discharge with good prognostic ability (AUC 0.769, AUC 0.703, and AUC 0.823, respectively). O/e LHR, liver position, and the combined predictive model were not predictive of ECMO requirement. In the right CDH patients, 33% survived to discharge, O/e LHR and liver position were not predictive of survival to discharge.

Conclusion

O/e LHR, liver position and the combination of these predictors, predicted survival to discharge in prenatally diagnosed left CDH with the combined model, the most predictive particularly in the isolated left CDH sub-group. Further analysis into effective predictors for ECMO requirement, and for right and complex left CDH is required.

title: Relative frequency of non-Wilms renal tumours in children: an institutional experience from a national tertiary referral centre in Malaysia.
abstract: Purpose International protocols for paediatric renal tumours are largely based on Western data with Wilms tumour (WT) accounting for more than 90% of cases. We aimed to evaluate the relative frequency of WT and Non-Wilms Renal Tumours (NWRTs) in a diverse Asian cohort in Malaysia. Methods A retrospective review was conducted of all primary paediatric renal tumours treated at a national tertiary referral centre from 2015 to 2024. Diagnosis was confirmed via post-operative histopathology. Results Of 95 children (median age 29 months), all were Asian descent (73.7% Malay, 9.5% Chinese, 6.3% Indian). WT accounted for only 68.4% of cases, while NWRTs accounted for 31.6%. Among NWRTs, 63.3% were malignant, primarily clear cell sarcoma of the kidney (CCSK, n = 7) and renal cell carcinoma (RCC, n = 4). In the classic WT age range (6-84 months), WT prevalence was only 75.6%, with CCSK representing 9.0%. Congenital mesoblastic nephroma (CMN) predominated in infants < 6 months (71.4%), while RCC was exclusively seen in children > 84 months (40.0%). Conclusion The substantial proportion of malignant NWRTs observed in this institutional cohort highlights potential risks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy without histological confirmation. Histopathological diagnosis via percutaneous core-needle biopsy or primary surgery may be highly considered in similar clinical settings.

title: [The eye as a mirror of the heart-retinal findings in heart failure and cardiovascular diseases].
abstract: Background Due to its unique anatomical and functional characteristics, the retina represents a promising organ for the evaluation of systemic vascular diseases. Modern imaging techniques, particularly optical coherence tomography angiography (OCT-A), enable noninvasive and quantitative assessment of retinal microcirculation. The aim of this review is to present current findings on the significance of retinal biomarkers in cardiovascular diseases, with a focus on heart failure. Results Numerous studies show associations between retinal vascular changes and arterial hypertension, coronary heart disease, left ventricular hypertrophy, and heart failure. Changes in retinal vascular parameters such as vascular density and perfusion density correlate with structural and functional cardiac changes. Patients with retinal vascular occlusions have an increased risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, and higher cardiovascular mortality. Initial studies in patients with acute decompensated heart failure have demonstrated changes in retinal vascular and perfusion density that can be reversed by recompensation. These observations led to the introduction of the term "cardio-ocular syndrome," which describes the interactions between cardiac function, systemic congestion, and retinal microcirculation. Conclusion Retinal imaging opens up new possibilities for the noninvasive assessment of systemic microcirculatory disorders in cardiovascular diseases. OCT‑A could contribute in the future to risk stratification, assessment of disease progression, and monitoring of therapy in heart failure.

title: Peripheral vessel tortuosity index and prognosis in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation.
abstract: Background and aims The peripheral vessel tortuosity index (TI) was proposed to discriminate procedural success in patients undergoing transcatheter endovascular aortic replacement but not in those undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). We aimed to investigate the TI and its prognostic relevance in patients undergoing transfemoral (Tf) TAVI. Methods Retrospective, observational single-center study, including patients undergoing Tf-TAVI from April 2011 to January 2023 at the TUM University Hospital, German Heart Centre, and available computed tomography angiography (CTA). Peripheral vessel measurements were performed using dedicated software (3mensio, Pie Medical). TI was determined dividing true central lumen vessel length from centerline reconstruction and direct distance from the aorto-iliac bifurcation to the epigastric artery. TI was dichotomized based on severity according to EVAR guidelines, where a TI of 1.5 is considered discriminatory for nonsevere tortuosity [< 1.5 for low TI (LTI)] and > 1.5 for high TI (HTI)]. Valve Academic Research Consortium 3 definitions were applied to describe procedural and follow-up outcomes. Mortality at 6-month follow-up was evaluated. Results We included 2002 patients. Overall age was 81 years [77, 85], 45.2% were female, EuroScore II was 4.22 [2.39, 7.60]. Age (p < 0.001), female sex (p < 0.001), diabetes (p < 0.001), peripheral artery disease (p = 0.002), myocardial infarction (p = 0.013), and creatinine (p = 0.001) were associated with tortuosity. Adjusted 6-month analysis showed that TI > 1.50 was associated with increased mortality [hazard ratio (HR) 1.679, 95% CI (1.098-2.567), p = 0.017]. Conclusions TI > 1.50 may determine a higher-risk population in patients undergoing Tf-TAVI. Further study is required to validate our findings.

title: [Cardiac involvement in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies].
abstract: Background Cardiac manifestations in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) occur more frequently than they are clinically recognized and are associated with increased morbidity and mortality. In particular, subclinical myocarditis often remains undetected due to nonspecific or absent symptoms. Objective This review aims to summarize the prevalence, pathophysiology, clinical spectrum, diagnostic strategies and therapeutic options of cardiac involvement in IIM and to provide practical recommendations for rheumatologists. Methods A scoping review on cardiac manifestations in IIM was performed. A structured literature search was conducted using the PubMed database. The search strategy included combinations of relevant keywords and MeSH terms. Primarily, English language original studies, systematic reviews and current guideline publications related to cardiac involvement in IIM were considered. Studies were selected based on clinical relevance, methodological quality and recency. Results The reported prevalence of cardiac involvement in IIM ranges from 4-26%, depending on the subtype and diagnostic approach. In addition to clinically overt myocarditis, subclinical abnormalities are common and can be detected in up to 50% of patients using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI). Pathophysiological mechanisms include immune-mediated myocardial injury, microvascular dysfunction and fibrotic remodelling. The initial diagnostic work-up should comprise taking a medical history, electrocardiography, measurement of cardiac biomarkers and echocardiography. The use of CMRI represents the diagnostic gold standard and enables sensitive detection of inflammatory and fibrotic myocardial changes. Therapeutically, early initiation of drug treatment, typically high-dose glucocorticoids combined with additional immunomodulating agents, constitutes the cornerstone of management. Conclusion Cardiac manifestations in IIM are common, prognostically relevant and frequently underestimated in clinical practice. A structured diagnostic approach with early use of CMRI and interdisciplinary management is essential to detect subclinical disease and guide appropriate treatment.
