title: Microenvironmental barriers to healing in osteoradionecrosis and opportunities for regenerative intervention.
abstract: Osteoradionecrosis (ORN) is a debilitating sequela of radiotherapy (RT) for head and neck cancer (HNC), characterized by persistent bone exposure or radiographic non-viability and profound tissue repair failure. Despite advances in radiation delivery and clinical management, ORN remains challenging to treat, with therapeutic strategies largely focused on symptom control, infection mitigation, or surgical reconstruction rather than restoration of regenerative capacity. Emerging evidence suggests that radiation-induced cellular senescence represents a central and underrecognized driver of ORN pathophysiology. Ionizing radiation disrupts the bone microenvironment through sustained vascular injury, impaired osteogenic-angiogenic coupling, chronic inflammation, and the accumulation of senescent bone-resident and stromal cells that secrete a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Together, these changes create a hostile niche that suppresses bone remodeling and wound healing long after radiation exposure. This review synthesizes current understanding of radiation-induced injury to the bone microenvironment, critically evaluates existing classification systems and treatment strategies for ORN, and examines emerging regenerative approaches. We further propose senotherapeutic strategies targeting radiation-induced cellular senescence as a complementary and potentially transformative avenue to restore tissue repair capacity. By integrating regenerative biomaterials with targeted modulation of senescence, future therapies may move beyond palliation toward true biological resolution of ORN. Biomaterial delivery systems (e.g., injectable hydrogels, mineral composite scaffolds, and cryogel platforms) are emerging as promising vehicles for spatiotemporally controlled senotherapeutic delivery within the irradiated bone niche.

title: From passive fillers to active implants: A 3D-printed trilayer piezoelectric scaffold recapitulating native bone hierarchy.
abstract: Critical-sized alveolar bone defects affect over 10 million patients annually, yet current synthetic bone substitutes act as passive osteoconductive fillers with unpredictable outcomes. Native bone, by contrast, achieves robust regeneration through a trilayered hierarchy of cancellous, cortical, and metabolically active periosteal tissues, with intrinsic piezoelectricity converting mechanical loading into endogenous electrical cues. While piezoelectric biomaterials have emerged as promising active implants, existing homogeneous scaffolds fail to recapitulate native bone's structural complexity and electromechanical coupling; to date, no work has combined this trilayer architecture with piezoelectric functionality in a single construct. Here we report a trilayer bioinspired piezoelectric scaffold fabricated via a two-step conformal 3D printing strategy, composed of a strontium-doped β-tricalcium phosphate (Sr-β-TCP) triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) cancellous layer, a dense cortical layer, and a barium titanate/silk fibroin (BTO/SF) piezoelectric periosteal layer. Under non-invasive low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) stimulation, the scaffold generates bioelectrical signals that support robust osteogenic activity and pro-angiogenic potential in vitro . Transcriptomic profiling reveals that these electrical cues are associated with intracellular calcium influx and upregulation of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/Akt) and Wnt/β-catenin pathways, consistent with enhanced osteogenic differentiation. In a critical-sized bone defect model, the trilayer scaffold with LIPUS achieves substantially superior bone regeneration relative to controls. This work pioneers the integration of native bone hierarchy with piezoelectric functionality into a single active construct, shifting bone tissue engineering from passive filling to bioelectric-guided repair. Coupling structural biomimicry with electroactive stimulation, this strategy holds potential for future bone regenerative applications, including alveolar bone reconstruction.

title: Oral squamous cell carcinoma: A modern review of pathogenesis and treatment.
abstract: Oral cancer (OC), predominantly oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), is a serious global health burden with high mortality rates, especially in South and Southeast Asia. OC is a severe worldwide health issue that is mostly caused by a sedentary lifestyle, alcohol, tobacco, and areca nut intake. The highest prevalence of OSCC is in India and Southeast Asia. Complex genomic and epigenetic changes, such as TP53 dysfunction, enhanced EGFR alteration, and dysregulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathways, in conjunction with tumor-promoting alterations in the tumor microenvironment, contribute to oral carcinogenesis ( Tan et al., 2023). Oral submucous fibrosis (a chronic condition that causes precancerous progression in mouth), and leukoplakia (white or gray patches to form on mucus membrane) are instances of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), which are key indicators of cancer conversion. Even with advances in histopathology and imaging, delayed diagnosis remains a major limitation. Salivary biomarkers, liquid biopsy devices, and artificial intelligence-based screening tools are examples of novel diagnostic methods with potential for early diagnosis. Therapeutically, novel approaches such as immunotherapy, targeted therapy, nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems, electro spun nanofibers, and plant-derived phytoformulations offer innovative, multi-targeted strategies with enhanced efficacy and reduce toxicity. However, surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy continue to be the primary treatment approaches. Improving new interventions for OC treatment needs a multifaceted approach that integrates early detection strategies, advanced therapeutic strategies, the use of plant-derived therapeutics, nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and public health awareness to get better therapeutic outcomes.

title: Radiosynthesis and preliminary evaluation of [ 11 C] and [ 18 F] labelled lacosamide scaffolds for brain PET imaging.
abstract: This study summarizes the automated, transition-metal-free radiosynthesis approach for producing [ 11 C]LCM and its bioisosteric analogue [ 18 F]FLCM, along with preliminary pharmacological and preclinical evaluations of these radiotracers can act as potent brain imaging radiotracer candidates. Radiosynthesis was carried out using an automated synthesis module targeting the terminal 3-oxy site of lacosamide. Physicochemical properties, including hydrophilic behavior and plasma-protein binding profile, were evaluated. Translational validation was performed via in vivo PET/CT imaging and ex vivo biodistribution in healthy Wistar rats. The synthesis module yielded a radiotracer with high radiochemical yield and radiochemical purity. Specific activity was determined to be ~21 .7GBq/μmol for [ 11 C]LCM and ~6.76 GBq/μmole for [ 18 F]FLCM. Both radiotracers show favorable hydrophilic and low PPB profiles. In vivo PET scan and ex vivo study confirmed the brain uptake, renal and hepatic clearance, and minimal off-target uptake. The favorable pharmaceutical profiles establish a promising baseline, further rigorous in vitro receptor-affinity assays and dynamic brain imaging in an animal model are required to validate the translational diagnostic utility of these radiotracers.

title: Mechanism‑targeted therapies for vestibular schwannoma: Emerging molecular pathways and translational horizons.
abstract: Vestibular schwannoma represents a significant clinical challenge characterized by hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, and cranial nerve morbidity. Despite advancements in surgery and radiotherapy, pharmacological options for recurrent, bilateral, or progressive disease remain limited. This review synthesizes current evidence on the molecular landscape of vestibular schwannoma, focusing on NF2 and Merlin inactivation as the upstream driver. We highlight how Merlin loss dysregulates interconnected signaling networks, specifically ErbB, PI3K Akt mTOR, MAPK, Hippo YAP TAZ, Wnt beta catenin, and NF kappaB. Furthermore, we examine how the tumor microenvironment, including tumor-associated macrophages, cancer associated fibroblasts, angiogenic mediators, and immune checkpoints, facilitates therapeutic resistance and immune evasion. The manuscript discusses the translational potential of diverse targeted inhibitors, including ErbB agents, mTOR inhibitors, and novel RNA based therapies such as circ 0001665. While bevacizumab remains the most clinically validated strategy for NF2related schwannomatosis (NF2-SWN), clinical responses are heterogeneous and durable efficacy is often elusive. We identify critical translational gaps, including the lack of predictive biomarkers and the limitations of current preclinical models in capturing the tumor microenvironment and tumor-induced hearing loss. Finally, we propose a precision medicine framework necessitating biomarker guided patient stratification, rational combination therapies targeting both intrinsic signaling and the microenvironment, and clinical trials that prioritize functional outcomes such as hearing preservation over radiographic response alone. This review provides a conceptual roadmap for transitioning toward mechanism guided treatment of vestibular schwannoma.

title: Anchoring nanozymes on microneedles via nanotemplate sacrificial synthesis for glutathione detection.
abstract: Region-specific dysregulation of glutathione (GSH) reflects neuropsychiatric disorders and tumor progression. Microscale precision sampling combined with timely monitoring of GSH provides region-specific molecular information that may aid in disease diagnosis. To enable minimally invasive brain-compatible intraoperative detection of GSH within a limited surgical time window, we designed a 5 mm × 5 mm on-surface microneedle nanozyme sensing platform by adopting a seed-mediated sacrificial template method. The peroxidase (POD)-like nanozyme Prussian blue (PB) probe was grown in situ on a sacrificial ZIF-67 nanotemplate, which was first anchored to the microneedle surface via in situ nucleation to prevent probe detachment in tissue. The dense PB coating substantially increases the immobilization efficiency of GSH aptamers, enabling selective in situ sampling and accumulation of GSH on the nanozyme. This creates a redox antagonistic effect between PB and GSH, which enables the platform to exhibit high selectivity toward GSH over common redox-active interferents. The quantitative concentration range of 271.3-900 μM (R 2 > 0.99) for GSH is demonstrated in a simulated gelatinous tissue, and GSH levels in brain interstitial fluid could be distinguished within 20 min. Less biopsy tissue and shorter analysis time may help minimize tissue damage and could provide timely intraoperative molecular information, potentially complementing histopathology.

The quantitative concentration range of 271.3-900 μM (R<sup>2</sup> > 0.99) for GSH is demonstrated in a simulated gelatinous tissue, and GSH levels in brain interstitial fluid could be distinguished within 20 min. Less biopsy tissue and shorter analysis time may help minimize tissue damage and could provide timely intraoperative molecular information, potentially complementing histopathology.

title: Orbitocranial resection for treatment of lacrimal gland malignant tumors with intracranial extension.
abstract: Objectives This study reports our experience with multidisciplinary surgical management of lacrimal gland malignant tumors with intracranial extension using the orbitocranial approach. Methods We reviewed treatment strategies and surgical approaches for lacrimal gland malignant tumors with intracranial extension and present 2 illustrative patients who underwent orbitocranial resection at our institution in 2015. Clinical records, radiographic images, histologic sections, and archived pathology specimens were reviewed. Results Both patients underwent orbitocranial tumor resection, followed by postoperative chemoradiotherapy. Orbital reconstruction was performed using a temporalis fascia flap and split calvarial bone grafts, with split-thickness skin grafting to line the orbital cavity. The follow-up periods were 69- and 66-months, respectively. Both patients remained alive without evidence of disease recurrence during follow-up. Conclusions The orbitocranial approach, combined with postoperative chemoradiotherapy, may provide satisfactory local and regional control in selected patients with lacrimal gland malignant tumors with intracranial extension. Long-term surveillance remains important because patients may remain at risk for disease recurrence or distant metastasis.

title: Ultrasound technologies to assess bone health: Past, present and future.
abstract: Background Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is currently the clinical reference standard for osteoporosis diagnosis and fracture risk assessment. However, it provides only a partial description of bone strength and has practical limitations related to accessibility and ionizing radiation. Over the past three decades, quantitative ultrasound (QUS) technologies have evolved from empirical heel-based measurements to advanced imaging approaches capable of characterizing cortical bone structure and material properties. Objectives To review the development of bone ultrasound technologies, summarize their clinical evidence for fracture risk assessment, and discuss the opportunities and challenges of emerging ultrasound-based approaches. Findings First-generation calcaneal QUS devices demonstrate fracture prediction comparable to peripheral DXA in large prospective studies and remain valuable for fracture risk assessment, particularly where DXA is unavailable or repeated X-ray examinations are undesirable. Their broader clinical adoption was limited mainly by device-specific algorithms, lack of standardization, and the absence of universally accepted diagnostic thresholds. Newer ultrasound technologies extend assessment to clinically relevant skeletal sites, including the hip and spine, or directly quantify cortical bone structure and material properties at peripheral sites. Radiofrequency echographic multi-spectrometry (REMS) has shown encouraging results in cross-sectional and prospective studies but relies on proprietary reference models and algorithms that require greater transparency and independent validation. Second-generation technologies, including cortical backscatter analysis (CortBS) and refraction-corrected imaging, provide quantitative measurements of cortical thickness, porosity-related microstructure, wave speed, attenuation and other biomechanical biomarkers in physical SI units, enabling independent validation and multiparametric fracture-risk modeling. However, until now these technologies have only been validated ex-vivo on human cadaver bones and in-vivo in small exploratory cross-sectional fracture discrimination studies. Multicenter cross-sectional and prospective studies are underway to create reference data and to establish their value for fracture risk prediction. Conclusions Bone ultrasound has progressed from an empirical screening tool to a family of quantitative technologies capable of assessing complementary aspects of bone quality and quantity. Calcaneal QUS is currently the only technology with an established guideline-recognized role in fracture risk assessment. Prospective multicenter fracture risk prediction studies, as well as technical standardization and transparent validation studies showing cross-vendor reproducibility and independent replication are now required to define the clinical role of newer ultrasound technologies and support their integration into future osteoporosis management and clinical routine use.

title: Quantification of bone loss, periosteal bone formation and novel histopathological changes in a mouse implant-related Staphylococcus aureus infection model.
abstract: Implant-associated bone infection involves a complex interplay between pathogenic stimuli and host cell responses, yet analysis in preclinical models has typically relied on qualitative or semi-quantitative measures. We aimed to establish a quantified evaluation framework to define host-pathogen relationships in a preclinical implant infection model. Staphylococcus aureus-coated stainless-steel implants were inserted trans-cortically in mouse tibiae and bone changes recorded longitudinally by in vivo micro-CT. An automated segmentation task list was developed to independently isolate and quantify cortical, periosteal-reactive, and trabecular bone compartments. RGB trichrome histomorphometry was used to quantify bone matrix integrity, osteocyte lacunar geometry, and osteoclastic activity. Droplet digital PCR was used to determine absolute bacterial and host genome copy number. Infected implants produced marked reductions in trabecular bone volume fraction, number, and bone mineral density (BMD), together with decreased cortical bone volume fraction and increased cortical porosity, accompanied by significant elevations in periosteal bone volume fraction. Histologically, infected bone exhibited increased eroded surface indicative of osteoclastic resorption, extensive degraded bone matrix and pathological remodelling of osteocyte lacunae toward circularity, consistent with an osteocytic osteolysis response. Infection-induced changes to cortical bone structure correlated mostly with host cell rather than bacterial load; however, cortical BMD negatively correlated with the bacterial:host genome ratio. This multifaceted, quantified framework reveals distinct pathobiological effects of implant-associated infection on trabecular, cortical, and periosteal bone compartments, bone matrix and osteocyte and osteoclast populations, consistent with reports in human patients, suggesting that major pathological changes are driven by the host bone cell response to infection.

title: Clinical phenotype and bone microarchitecture of cutaneous-skeletal hypophosphatemia syndrome: experience from a single center in China.
abstract: Context Cutaneous-skeletal hypophosphatemia syndrome (CSHS) is a rare mosaic RASopathy characterized by epidermal or melanocytic nevi, skeletal dysplasia, and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23)-mediated hypophosphatemic rickets. However, its bone microarchitectural features remain underdefined. Objectives The study aimed to characterize the clinical, genetic, and skeletal microarchitectural features of CSHS. Methods We summarized clinical findings of 6 CSHS patients with genetically confirmed somatic RAS mutations. Skeletal involvement was assessed by whole-body bone scintigraphy. High-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography parameters at the distal radius and tibia were compared with age- and sex-matched XLH controls (1:3). Literature review of 24 genetically confirmed CSHS patients was performed to assess genotype-phenotype correlation. Results All patients were confirmed to carry somatic HRAS or NRAS mutation in affected skin. Hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase and elevated FGF23 were found in all patients. Genotype-phenotype correlation analysis did not identify any significant biochemical or systemic burden differences across 3 genotypes. Compared with XLH controls, CSHS patients exhibited significantly reduced total and trabecular volumetric BMD (vBMD), with relatively preserved cortical vBMD. Bone cross-sectional geometry was less expanded than in XLH at the tibia. In addition, thinner trabeculae with greater separation were found at the radius, and the distal tibia showed thinner cortices and decreased cortical porosity. Estimated bone stiffness and failure load were significantly lower at both the radius and tibia. Conclusions CSHS is associated with pronounced trabecular vBMD impairment and reduced bone strength compared with XLH controls. These findings are consistent with a combined contribution of intrinsic skeletal dysplasia and chronic hypophosphatemia on bone, although further studies are needed to elucidate these mechanisms.

title: Preliminary study on early microvascular ingrowth into distracted callus during distraction osteogenesis-A non-invasive approach to explore the early growth patterns and possible mechanism of distraction osteogenesis in vivo.
abstract: Background Distraction osteogenesis (DO) is critical for repairing large segmental bone defects. Early callus vascularization is essential for bone regeneration; however, real-time microcirculatory assessment remains lacking. This study aimed to elucidate spatiotemporal microvascular network construction in distracted callus using super-resolution contrast-enhanced ultrasound (SR CEUS) and high-frame-rate contrast-enhanced ultrasound (HiFR CEUS) in a sheep tibial DO model. Methods Six sheep underwent tibial DO. On day 7 of distraction, B-mode ultrasound, "Firefly" imaging, SR CEUS, and HiFR CEUS were performed. Quantitative parameters including vessel density (VD), perfusion index (PI), mean intensity, and peak intensity (PKI) were compared among three regions: central high-perfusion area (CHPA), annular low-perfusion area (ALPA), and peripheral high-perfusion area (PHPA). Results B-mode ultrasound revealed outward bulging of distracted callus. "Firefly" imaging detected microcalcifications. title: Immediate high-dose-rate brachytherapy with volumetric planning for keloids: Clinical outcomes.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate clinical outcomes and toxicity of a standardized protocol of immediate (<6 h postoperative) high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy with volumetric planning in patients with keloids. Methods and materials We conducted a retrospective cohort study including consecutive patients with histologically confirmed keloids treated with surgical excision followed by immediate (<6 h) HDR brachytherapy between April 2014 and November 2025. Treatment was delivered using a uniform fractionation scheme of 12 Gy in three fractions. CT-based planning was performed in all cases, and the clinical target volume (CTV) was defined over the surgical bed. Dosimetric analysis included D90 as the primary coverage parameter. The primary endpoint was local control (LC), defined as recurrence-free interval. Secondary endpoints included late toxicity (RTOG/EORTC) and patient-reported outcomes assessed using the POSAS 3.0 scale. Results A total of 64 keloids were included. Median follow-up was 37.5 months. The overall local control rate was 92.2%, with five recurrences (7.8%), all occurring within the first 24 months. Median D90 was 98.5%. Larger lesions (>5 cm) showed a higher recurrence rate compared to smaller lesions (12.5% vs. 7.1%). No acute toxicity was observed. Late toxicity was limited to mild hypopigmentation (9.4%), grade one telangiectasia (6.3%), and superficial atrophy (4.7%). One case of mild chondritis (1.5%) was reported. Patient-reported outcomes demonstrated minimal residual symptoms and favorable aesthetic and functional outcomes, as reflected by the patient-reported POSAS scores CONCLUSIONS: Immediate (<6 h) HDR brachytherapy with volumetric planning provides high local control and favorable toxicity in keloid treatment. A regimen of 12 Gy in three fractions is feasible and well-tolerated, representing a valid option in the multidisciplinary management of keloids.

title: Deep learning-assisted needle artifact suppression for enhanced anatomical visualization in prostate high-dose-rate brachytherapy ultrasound imaging.
abstract: Purpose Implanted needles introduce acoustic artifacts that degrade transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) images during high-dose-rate (HDR) prostate brachytherapy, complicating ultrasound-only contouring. We developed an artificial intelligence (AI) needle eraser to remove needles and associated artifacts and facilitate structure delineation. Methods TRUS images from 120 patients undergoing HDR prostate brachytherapy were retrospectively collected. Three-dimensional volumes were acquired immediately before and after needle insertion. A Cycle Generative Adversarial Network (CycleGAN) was trained to transform postneedle images into needle-free images. Two physicians independently rated clinical utility for prostate and urethra delineation using a four-point scale (1 = poor; 4 = excellent). Prostate and urethra contours from preneedle and needle-erased images were compared with clinical reference contours using Dice similarity coefficient (DSC). Results The AI tool suppressed needles and associated artifacts, improving visualization of the prostate and urethral lumen. Mean reader scores were 3.80 ± 0.43 for prostate and 3.75 ± 0.37 for urethra delineation. Compared with preneedle contours, needle-erased contours showed higher agreement with clinical references: prostate DSC increased from 0.91 to 0.93, and urethra DSC increased from 0.70 to 0.89. Conclusions A CycleGAN-based needle eraser can generate needle-free ultrasound images from postinsertion scans and improve visualization and contour agreement for physician delineation.

title: Early postnatal brain volumes and two-year cognitive outcomes in preterm infants: An exploratory machine learning study.
abstract: Introduction Premature birth is associated with an increased risk of cognitive and motor developmental problems. Early prediction of these outcomes is crucial for timely intervention and adequate follow-up. This study aimed to predict cognitive and motor outcomes in preterm-born infants using brain volumetric features in combination with clinical and demographic perinatal characteristics, and to compare the performance of three different machine learning algorithms. Methods We acquired quantitative structural brain MRI at approximately 30 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA) and clinical and demographic birth characteristics including gestational age, sex, birthweight, and maternal education level. Machine learning techniques were applied to predict cognitive (N = 63) and motor (N = 41) outcomes at two years corrected age, assessed using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development III, in infants born before 30 weeks gestation. We evaluated the performance of logistic regression, linear support vector classifier (linear SVC), and k-nearest neighbour (KNN). Results Employing volumetric features only, KNN achieved a validation accuracy of 0.64, showing modest predictive power for cognitive outcomes. Adding clinical characteristics did not significantly improve accuracy. The models did not perform better than chance when predicting motor outcomes. Conclusion Volumetric features demonstrated modest predictive ability for cognitive outcomes, and the addition of clinical features did not significantly improve performance. The low to moderate overall validation accuracy underscores, however, the challenges faced in the clinical application of machine learning in neuroimaging. The reliability and clinical applicability of predictions of outcomes from advanced neuroimaging data will largely depend on the quantity and quality of the data, methodological standardisation, and the generalisability of the prediction models.

title: Biomechanical insights into traumatic brain injury in Females: Current understanding and future directions.
abstract: The incidence of traumatic brain injury (TBI) in females has increased in recent decades, driven by socioeconomic changes and greater participation in high-risk activities. This rise, combined with the historically limited availability of experimental data from female subjects, highlights the pressing need to improve both the quantity and quality of sex-specific data. Research has identified systematic differences between males and females in brain volume, tissue stiffness, and gray/white matter composition. While differences in brain size are often linked to body dimensions, sex-specific disparities in biomechanical properties, such as viscoelasticity and regional stiffness, may influence TBI susceptibility. Imaging-based techniques, particularly Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE), have revealed that female brains tend to exhibit higher stiffness in regions like the occipital and temporal lobes, suggesting a differential biomechanical response to TBI. These regional differences may also serve as potential biomarkers for the diagnosis, monitoring, and tracking the progression of neurodegenerative diseases such as multiple sclerosis, aiding in the assessment of disease progression and therapeutic response. Despite these insights, most current finite element head models (FEHMs) rely on population-averaged parameters that may not adequately represent female-specific tissue mechanics. This review highlights the need to incorporate sex-specific mechanical properties into numerical simulations to improve the accuracy of TBI risk assessments and injury prediction. We emphasize the need for future studies using imaging, experimental methods, and computational modeling to better understand the biomechanical behavior of female brain tissue. Such efforts are essential for advancing personalized approaches to brain injury prevention, diagnosis, and treatment in females.

title: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals vascular heterogeneity and cell-cell communication remodeling in the glioma blood-tumor barrier.
abstract: Background The blood-brain barrier (BBB) restricts drug delivery in glioma, yet its pathologically remodeled counterpart, the blood-tumor barrier (BTB), is a promising therapeutic target. A comprehensive view of the cellular composition and transcriptional heterogeneity of the vascular compartment across the BBB-to-BTB transition is essential for improving glioma therapy. Methods We performed a secondary single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis of the public GSE242044 dataset (7 patients; 13 tumor and adjacent non-tumor surgical specimens, comprising IDH-mutant lower-grade gliomas and IDH-wild-type gliomas). After stringent quality control, doublet removal, Harmony batch correction, and annotation with SingleR plus canonical markers, we dissected vascular cell heterogeneity and performed differential expression, Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA), pseudotime (Monocle/Slingshot), and CellChat ligand-receptor inference, with sample-level statistical comparisons (Kruskal-Wallis and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests on per-specimen values). Findings were assessed in three independent glioma scRNA-seq cohorts (GSE162631, GSE117891, GSE174554) and in the CGGA bulk cohort. Results Vascular cell composition (relative representation among the profiled vascular-enriched cells) showed trends across conditions: endothelial cells declined from 60.6 % to 47.5 %, whereas pericytes (15.8 % to 18.0 %) and immune cells increased in IDH-wild-type tumors (macrophages 1.3 % to 7.0 %; T cells 3.0 % to 7.5 %); astrocytes increased from 1.1 % to 4.5 %; these specimen-level trends were mostly not statistically significant (Supplementary Table S1). Cell-cell communication was predicted to be rewired, shifting from pericyte-smooth muscle cell crosstalk in non-tumor and IDH-mutant tissues toward pericyte-astrocyte and predicted vascular-immune interactions in IDH-wild-type tumors. Differential expression and enrichment analyses identified an IDH-wild-type vascular program dominated by extracellular matrix remodeling (COL1A1, COL3A1, COL4A1, LAMB1, TIMP1) and angiogenic activation (ANGPT2), with loss of quiescent endothelial markers (CA4, KLF2). Candidate markers (COL1A1, COL3A1, F3, S100A4, CSPG4, ANGPT2) showed no consistent prognostic association across independent cohorts. Conclusions This secondary analysis delineates transcriptional heterogeneity of BBB/BTB vascular cells and their inferred communication remodeling in glioma. The identified subtype markers are candidate biomarkers that require independent validation; our findings provide a framework for future studies-including spatial and protein-level validation of the candidate markers, functional permeability and coculture assays of the predicted vascular-immune interactions, and preclinical testing of BTB-modulating delivery strategies such as focused-ultrasound-mediated opening in glioma models.

The blood-brain barrier (BBB) restricts drug delivery in glioma, yet its pathologically remodeled counterpart, the blood-tumor barrier (BTB), is a promising therapeutic target. A comprehensive view of the cellular composition and transcriptional heterogeneity of the vascular compartment across the BBB-to-BTB transition is essential for improving glioma therapy.

Methods

We performed a secondary single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis of the public GSE242044 dataset (7 patients; 13 tumor and adjacent non-tumor surgical specimens, comprising IDH-mutant lower-grade gliomas and IDH-wild-type gliomas). After stringent quality control, doublet removal, Harmony batch correction, and annotation with SingleR plus canonical markers, we dissected vascular cell heterogeneity and performed differential expression, Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA), pseudotime (Monocle/Slingshot), and CellChat ligand-receptor inference, with sample-level statistical comparisons (Kruskal-Wallis and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests on per-specimen values). Findings were assessed in three independent glioma scRNA-seq cohorts (GSE162631, GSE117891, GSE174554) and in the CGGA bulk cohort.

Results

Vascular cell composition (relative representation among the profiled vascular-enriched cells) showed trends across conditions: endothelial cells declined from 60.6 % to 47.5 %, whereas pericytes (15.8 % to 18.0 %) and immune cells increased in IDH-wild-type tumors (macrophages 1.3 % to 7.0 %; T cells 3.0 % to 7.5 %); astrocytes increased from 1.1 % to 4.5 %; these specimen-level trends were mostly not statistically significant (Supplementary Table S1). Cell-cell communication was predicted to be rewired, shifting from pericyte-smooth muscle cell crosstalk in non-tumor and IDH-mutant tissues toward pericyte-astrocyte and predicted vascular-immune interactions in IDH-wild-type tumors. Differential expression and enrichment analyses identified an IDH-wild-type vascular program dominated by extracellular matrix remodeling (COL1A1, COL3A1, COL4A1, LAMB1, TIMP1) and angiogenic activation (ANGPT2), with loss of quiescent endothelial markers (CA4, KLF2). Candidate markers (COL1A1, COL3A1, F3, S100A4, CSPG4, ANGPT2) showed no consistent prognostic association across independent cohorts.

Conclusions

This secondary analysis delineates transcriptional heterogeneity of BBB/BTB vascular cells and their inferred communication remodeling in glioma. The identified subtype markers are candidate biomarkers that require independent validation; our findings provide a framework for future studies-including spatial and protein-level validation of the candidate markers, functional permeability and coculture assays of the predicted vascular-immune interactions, and preclinical testing of BTB-modulating delivery strategies such as focused-ultrasound-mediated opening in glioma models.

title: Distinctive patterns of right-hemisphere vulnerability in cerebral small vessel disease: a gray matter asymmetry study.
abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a leading cause of vascular cognitive impairment (VCI), characteristically associated with gray matter (GM) loss. However, it remains unclear whether this GM loss exhibits regional interhemispheric asymmetry and how it relates to cognitive function. In this study, 56 CSVD patients and 56 demographically matched healthy controls were included, and structural MRI as well as cognitive and clinical data were collected. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and the GM Asymmetry Index (GMAI; calculated as (L-R)/(L + R), higher values indicate relatively greater left-sided GM) were performed using a study-specific symmetric template. Perivascular spaces were also estimated with a deep learning framework. Partial correlations were tested against multi-domain cognitive performance. Compared with controls, CSVD patients exhibited extensive GM reduction in the right superior and middle frontal gyri as well as in the left hippocampus and putamen. Regional GMAI analyses further suggested altered hemispheric GM loss, with leftward shifts (higher GMAI) in the middle temporal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, and precuneus, and rightward shifts (lower GMAI) in the inferior temporal and fusiform gyri. Additionally, subcortical nuclei exhibited a corresponding leftward lateralization of perivascular space burden. Association analyses showed that right prefrontal volume was positively related to global cognitive scores, whereas left temporal asymmetry tracked cognitive decline. Of note, this right-dominant pattern in prefrontal-related regions is consistent with our activation likelihood estimation meta-analytic re-synthesis of prior VBM evidence and NeuroSynth mapping. Collectively, these findings suggest a distinct topographical vulnerability of the right hemisphere in CSVD and highlight GMAI as a neuroimaging marker for vascular cognitive decline.

title: Mechanomarker-informed identification of Alzheimer's disease based on lateral ventricular deformation.
abstract: Structural magnetic resonance imaging reveals lateral ventricular enlargement as a prominent structural change in normal aging, with accelerated expansion in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. In this study, we characterize ventricular shape changes and corresponding mechanical loading in cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects in their seventies, using longitudinal magnetic resonance images over a two-year interval. Surface-based deformation metrics were computed to capture localized displacement magnitude, curvature changes, surface area stretch, and maximum principal wall strain, both relative to the population average at baseline and relative to each subject's baseline over the two-year follow-up. Longitudinal displacement over two years increased markedly with disease progression, rising 114 ± 15% from CN to AD. Area stretch exhibited a more modest 6 ± 1% increase, while maximum principal wall strain nearly doubled, increasing 110 ± 16% from CN to AD. Curvature change remained minimal when averaged globally, although localized deformations along ventricular edges suggest subtle region-specific alterations. The significant differences between mechanics-related features for individual disease groups highlight the value of deformation-derived mechanomarkers that go beyond the more commonly reported volumetric analyses. As such, our mechanomarkers demonstrated a predictive value for disease classification, especially in the direct comparison of CN and AD. Our results highlight the potential of ventricular mechanomarkers as non-invasive, MRI-derived biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of neurodegenerative progression, providing insight into the mechanical loading resulting from structural brain shape changes.

title: Diffusion MRI Assessment of White Matter Microstructure and Free-Water Fraction in Drug-Naïve Children with SeLECTS.
abstract: Background Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS) is a common childhood-onset focal epilepsy syndrome. Although seizures are typically self-limited, some children may show neurodevelopmental or cognitive vulnerability. Diffusion MRI may provide insight into white matter alterations in SeLECTS. Objective To evaluate white matter diffusion differences in newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) and white matter free-water fraction (FW-WM), and to explore within-patient associations with selected seizure-related and cognitive variables. Methods Fifty-three newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS and 53 healthy controls with a similar age and sex distribution were prospectively enrolled in this cross-sectional case-control study. Diffusion MRI was acquired at 3.0T, and white matter diffusion differences were assessed using TBSS and FW-WM analyses. Voxelwise between-group differences in fractional anisotropy (FA) were tested with age and sex as covariates and corrected using threshold-free cluster enhancement-based family-wise error correction. FW-WM was compared between groups using age- and sex-adjusted general linear models, with additional adjustment for years of education in a sensitivity analysis. Exploratory within-patient associations between imaging measures and selected clinical or cognitive variables were assessed using partial Spearman correlations with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Children with SeLECTS showed lower FA than healthy controls in multiple TBSS-defined white matter regions after correction for multiple comparisons, mainly involving commissural, projection, and association pathways. No between-group differences in mean, axial, or radial diffusivity survived correction for multiple comparisons. FW-WM was higher in the SeLECTS group after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted mean difference = 0.0085; 95% CI, 0.0023 to 0.0147; P = 0.008), with similar results after additional adjustment for education. In exploratory cluster-level analyses, mean FA in a left-sided cluster involving the posterior internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, and sagittal stratum was inversely associated with disease duration after FDR correction (r = -0.413; P = 0.003; q = 0.010). No imaging-cognition or within-patient FW-WM-FA association survived FDR correction. Conclusions Newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS showed white matter diffusion differences, including lower FA in distributed TBSS-defined regions and higher FW-WM. These findings support diffusion MRI-based characterization of white matter alterations at diagnosis, before antiseizure treatment. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify their clinical and developmental relevance.

title: Fetal Brain Volumes in Complete Vascular Ring: A Cross-Sectional MRI Study.
abstract: Background The association between complete vascular ring (CVR) and prenatal brain development remains poorly characterized. Objective To compare global and regional fetal brain volumes between fetuses with CVR and controls, accounting for gestational age (GA), fetal sex, and estimated fetal weight. Methods In this retrospective single-center study, 70 prenatally diagnosed CVR fetuses and 200 GA-matched controls with normal brain anatomy (22-37 weeks) underwent 1.5-T fetal MRI. Motion-corrected three-dimensional brain reconstructions were generated by slice-to-volume registration, and 19 regions were automatically segmented using a deep-learning pipeline. Linear regression included continuous GA, group, their interaction, fetal sex, and estimated fetal weight. Regional-to-intracranial volume ratios and sensitivity analyses incorporating maternal body mass index were evaluated. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Results At the 28-week reference age, adjusted supratentorial brain, cortical gray matter, white matter, thalamic, lentiform nucleus, brainstem, and lateral ventricular volumes were smaller in the CVR group (all false-discovery-rate-adjusted P<0.05). Intracranial volume did not differ significantly. Thalamic, lentiform nucleus, brainstem, and lateral ventricular proportions were also smaller. No group-by-GA interaction survived correction in the primary model. Conclusions CVR was associated with differences in selected fetal brain volumes, including regional differences relative to intracranial volume. Larger longitudinal studies with postnatal follow-up are needed.

title: Recent progress in the biomarkers of peripheral artery disease.
abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a prevalent atherosclerotic disorder affecting over 113 million individuals worldwide, with its global burden projected to rise substantially amid population aging and increasing metabolic comorbidities, including type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Conventional diagnostic assessment, including the ankle-brachial index (ABI) as a non-invasive hemodynamic measurement and imaging-based techniques such as duplex ultrasonography, computed tomography angiography, magnetic resonance angiography, and digital subtraction angiography, has limited sensitivity for early disease detection and does not fully capture the multidimensional pathophysiological processes underlying disease progression, and ABI generates false-negative results in elderly and diabetic patients with medial arterial calcification, a critical unaddressed limitation in routine screening. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies have accelerated the discovery of circulating biomarkers that reflect distinct pathological axes-inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and metabolic dysregulation-underlying PAD pathogenesis. These novel biomarkers hold considerable promise for enhancing early diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostic assessment, therapeutic monitoring and postoperative restenosis prediction, and individualized precision intervention guidance. This review systematically summarizes the most recent advances in PAD biomarkers across these four pathophysiological categories, elucidating their mechanistic links to disease progression and critically evaluating their clinical utility and translational barriers; We further develop population-specific biomarker strategies for patients with diabetes mellitus, dialysis-dependent kidney disease, and chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), while considering disease-specific confounding factors and the current limitations of biomarker validation. We further discuss emerging biomarker classes, including extracellular vesicle-derived molecules and microRNAs, and highlight the superior diagnostic and predictive efficacy of multi-biomarker panels compared with single indicators, combined with machine learning modeling frameworks. Large-scale multi-center, multi-ethnic prospective validation studies, standardized pre-analytical and analytical detection protocols, and cost-effectiveness health economic evaluations remain essential prerequisites for full-scale clinical implementation.

title: Synbiotic to Attenuate Resorption of the Skeleton (STARS): Design and participant recruitment of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to test the efficacy of SBD111 medical food in older women.
abstract: Osteoporosis and related fractures pose a costly public health challenge. Primary prevention of bone loss is largely limited to non-pharmacologic options without consistent guidelines. Prior studies have demonstrated that modification of the gut microbiome can influence bone homeostasis. The Synbiotic To Attenuate Resorption of the Skeleton (STARS) trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and mechanistic effects of daily intake of SBD111, a fruit and vegetable-derived synbiotic medical food on the skeleton, gut microbiome, and inflammation biomarkers in women aged ≥60 years. This 18-month, investigator-initiated, single-site, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial had an enrollment goal of 220 women, a primary endpoint of proportionate change in lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD) relative to baseline, and secondary outcomes including Quantitative Computed Tomography derived volumetric BMD and vertebral compressive strength, gut microbiome function, and bone and inflammatory biomarkers. Recruitment approaches included simultaneous digital and traditional methods beginning August 2024. As of July 2025, there were 42 enrolled participants (32 via digital, 10 via traditional); baseline demographics, eligibility, and enrollment rates were similar across recruitment strategies. Digital recruitment achieved over three times faster enrollment (2.9 vs. 0.9 enrollments/month) and was nearly 10 times more staff-efficient (0.05 vs. 0.48 cumulative weekly full-time equivalent) despite greater cost per enrollment ($548 vs. $173). These findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of digital recruitment of older adults, offering valuable insights for future nutrition and microbiome clinical trials. The STARS trial is positioned to provide high-quality evidence for skeletal health maintenance in older women using SBD111.

title: CEUS- versus US- and CT-guided Biopsy for Subpleural Lung Lesions: A Prospective, Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Background Ultrasound (US)-guided percutaneous lung needle biopsy (PLNB), the guideline-recommended approach for subpleural lung lesion (SLL) diagnosis, requires comparison with CT-guided biopsy based on high-level evidence clinical studies. Research question Is US-guided PLNB superior to CT-guided biopsy in diagnostic performance and safety, and does CEUS provide further advantages? Study design and methods Participants undergoing PLNB for SLLs between June 2020 and November 2023 were randomized to US-, CEUS- and CT-guided biopsies. The dual primary outcomes were diagnostic yield and disease-specific diagnostic sensitivity. Diagnostic yield was defined according to the strict ATS/ACCP definition as the proportion of biopsies yielding clinically actionable diagnoses, while sensitivity referred to the proportion of patients with a confirmed disease correctly identified by biopsy. Four secondary outcomes included complication rate, CNB/FNA utilization, puncture number, and puncture time, with the overall complication rate adopted as the key safety indicator. Results A total of 2485 participants were randomized into the US (n=828), CEUS (n=829) and CT (n=828) groups. The CEUS-guided biopsy achieved the highest diagnostic yield (CEUS: 88.8%[736/829] vs. CT: 78.9%[653/828] vs. US: 76.0%[629/828], χ 2 =49.046, P <0.001) , as well as the highest diagnostic sensitivity (CEUS: 86.1%[714/829] vs. CT: 74.3%[615/828] vs. US: 68.7%[569/828], χ 2 =72.623, P <0.001). For disease-specific analysis, CEUS yielded superior diagnostic sensitivity for malignant subtypes (CEUS: 91.8%[563/613] vs. CT: 83.2%[520/625] vs. US: 75.2%[479/637], χ 2 =62.259, P <0.001) and specific benign disorders (CEUS: 69.9%[151/216] vs. CT: 46.8%[95/203] vs. US: 47.1%[90/191], χ 2 =29.712, P <0.001). Furthermore, the CEUS group exhibited the lowest overall complication rate (CEUS: 4.6%[38/828] vs. US: 7.5%[60/802] vs. CT: 15.8%[127/805], χ 2 =65.322, P <0.001). Interpretation For SLL biopsy, CEUS-guided PLNB outperforms US- and CT-guided approaches in both diagnostic performance and procedural safety. CEUS guidance notably improves disease-specific diagnostic sensitivity for malignant subtypes and specific benign pulmonary disorders, serving as an optimal technique for clinical percutaneous lung biopsy. Clinical trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry; No.: ChiCTR2100045374; URL: www.chictr.org.cn.

title: Determinants of lung cancer screening follow-up care in community care settings: A qualitative multi-case study in the ACCELL trial.
abstract: Background Adherence to lung cancer screening (LCS) follow-up is essential to achieve mortality benefits from screening. However, population-based studies demonstrate follow-up is <50% in clinical settings. Determinants (barriers and facilitators) of LCS follow-up in community settings are under-studied. Research question What are determinants of LCS follow-up in community settings? Study design and methods This qualitative multi-case study informed a pre-post intervention trial, testing pragmatic interventions to address LCS follow-up in community settings. We conducted rapid ethnographic assessments (REA) through virtual and in person site visits of LCS delivery in three community-based healthcare systems in Washington state. Additionally at the two future intervention sites, we conducted provider and patient interviews. Interview transcripts were analyzed using Rapid Group Analysis Process. All data were triangulated according to Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities Research Framework domains. Results Twenty-eight organizational leaders, providers, and staff participated in REA. Thirty-one patients and 15 providers from the future intervention sites participated in interviews. Determinants of LCS follow-up in the intervention domain included role of primary care, LCS complexity and care process standardization. In the inner setting domain (organization and clinic), screening prioritization, EHR use, radiology support, and context of wellness visits affected LCS. The main theme in the outer setting domain was the influence of social determinants of health on LCS. In the individuals domain, shared beliefs in LCS and LCS education and information sharing were key. In the process implementation domain, clinical champions and use of data and metrics were crucial. Interpretation Integrated findings suggest determinants related to LCS complexity, care fragmentation, socioeconomic status and language, and limitations of PCPs could be overcome through more centralized approaches. However, increased use of EHR tools, increased education and standardizing LCS performance metrics may enable follow-up in decentralized settings. Clinical trials registration NCT06324110.

title: Molecular surveillance of adenovirus and coronavirus in Procellariiformes, Brazil: Detection of new divergent adenoviruses.
abstract: Adenoviruses are widespread DNA viruses that infect a broad range of vertebrate hosts and are recognized for their long-term host coevolution, remarkable genetic diversity, and broad pathogenic potential. Coronaviruses circulate among wild birds due to their evolutionary potential and are relevant to animal and public health. However, the diversity and ecological role of these viruses in pelagic seabirds remain poorly understood. This study provides the first molecular survey of adenoviruses and coronaviruses in Procellariiformes from the South Atlantic. Fifty stranded individuals representing 12 Procellariiformes species were collected along the southeastern Brazilian coast, between 2017 and 2023. Adenovirus and coronavirus survey were performed using nested PCR protocols, followed by sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and histopathology of positive cases. Adenovirus was detected in seven individuals (14%; 95% CI: 5.8-26.7%) from three species: Southern Giant Petrels (Macronectes giganteus), Cory's Shearwaters (Calonectris borealis), and Black-browed Albatrosses (Thalassarche melanophris). Five sequence types were identified, including similar variants in Southern Giant Petrels and distinct adenoviruses in Cory's Shearwaters and Black-browed Albatrosses. All viruses clustered within a divergent lineage with adenoviruses previously detected in New Zealand seabirds and a Chimney Swift from the USA. No intranuclear inclusion bodies were found in histopathological analysis. All specimens were coronavirus-negative. This first molecular detection of adenoviruses in Procellariiformes expands the known diversity and host range of seabird adenoviruses and suggests circulation of genetically distinct viruses across oceanic regions, highlighting the need for genomic and epidemiological studies of their evolution, transmission, and health impacts.

title: Intraoperative endoscopy in colorectal surgery in Spain: Results of a national survey.
abstract: Introduction Anastomotic leakage remains one of the most feared complications in colorectal surgery. Intraoperative colonoscopy (IOC) enables direct assessment of anastomotic integrity and allows immediate therapeutic intervention. The aim of this study is to describe the implementation of intraoperative endoscopy in colorectal surgery in Spain, analysing available resources, training, utilization patterns, and impact on intraoperative decision-making. Methods Observational, descriptive, cross-sectional study based on an online survey distributed through the Asociación Española de Cirugía. The questionnaire, validated by a panel of experts, comprised 26 questions grouped into five domains: professional profile, infrastructure, technique and protocols, perceived outcomes, and training. The survey was active for 46 days. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed using absolute frequencies and percentages. Results A total of 122 complete responses were obtained from 92 hospitals across 16 autonomous communities (completion rate: 31.7%). Flexible endoscopy was used by 55.7% of respondents, and 36.1% performed IOC routinely. Surgeons performed the procedures in 61.5% of cases. IOC was also used for localisation of lesions by 54.9% of respondents. In 61.8% of surgeons, the surgical approach was modified in up to 20% of patients. Indocyanine green fluorescence angiography was available in 85.2% of centres. Overall, 86.1% considered IOC a fundamental tool, and complications were virtually absent. Conclusions IOC is highly regarded in Spain, yet its systematic integration remains heterogeneous. Deficits in structured training, therapeutic methods, and equipment persist. A joint effort from scientific societies, hospital management, and surgical teams is required to ensure uniform implementation and improve anastomotic safety.

title: Modern multidisciplinary management of brain metastasis.
abstract: Brain metastases (BrM) are no longer considered to be a uniform end-stage complication of cancer, but as a biologically and clinically heterogeneous disease requiring coordinated management. This article synthesises the fundamentals of BrM diagnosis and treatment, relevant to primary and urgent care settings. Treatment sequencing should account for acuity of neurologic symptoms, anticipated intracranial response, extracranial disease tempo, steroid requirements, and risks of local therapy. Focal radiotherapy is now the dominant local modality for limited BrM. Surgery remains central for large, symptomatic, diagnostically uncertain, or mass-effect-producing lesions. Postoperative stereotactic radiosurgery is favoured over whole-brain radiotherapy. Novel CNS-active targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors can permit deferral of radiotherapy in carefully selected asymptomatic patients with certain molecularly defined cancers. Follow-up, based on longitudinal MRI, requires multi-disciplinary surveillance and decision-making. Optimal care combines integrated multi-disciplinary management and risk-adapted sequencing to jointly achieve preservation of neurologic function while maintaining durable systemic control.

title: Evaluating skeletal muscle in chronic liver disease: remaining challenges.
abstract: Skeletal muscle alterations are increasingly recognized as determinants of prognosis in chronic liver disease, and computed tomography (CT) has made their assessment widely accessible. However, interpretation of these measurements raises several challenges. First, myosteatosis is usually inferred from low CT muscle attenuation, which has not been validated against intramuscular fat content in cirrhosis. Second, muscle alterations may differ according to the aetiology of liver disease, and studies pooling aetiologies may obscure aetiology-specific patterns. Third, "sarcopenia" is frequently incorrectly used for low muscle mass alone, whereas incorporating muscle function, better predicts adverse outcomes in chronic liver disease. Addressing these issues is necessary before muscle quality can become a reliable clinical biomarker.

title: A multimodal MRI radiomics sonata for differentiating small renal masses: a two-center retrospective study.
abstract: Background Accurately distinguishing benign from malignant small renal masses (SRMs) is crucial to avoid unnecessary surgeries, yet reliable preoperative diagnostic tools remain limited. Methods A total of 189 patients with SRMs from two hospitals (2018-2022) were enrolled. Clinical data and MRI features were analyzed by two radiologists. Radiomics features were automatically extracted from manually segmented ROIs using dedicated software. Significant features were selected via univariate analysis, multivariate regression, and Lasso to develop three models: radiomics, clinical, and combined nomogram. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using the Area Under the receiver operating characteristic Curve (AUC). Results The radiomics-clinical nomogram was constructed using T2WI signal intensity (p < 0.001), pseudocapsule (p = 0.001), and radiomics score (Rad-score, p = 0.001) via multivariate logistic regression. In the training set, the nomogram achieved an AUC of 0.962 (95% CI: 0.931-0.993), outperforming both the radiomics model (AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.862-0.974) and the clinical model (AUC = 0.856, 95% CI: 0.780-0.933). Favorable performance was observed in the internal validation set (nomogram: AUC = 0.981, 95% CI: 0.944-1.000; radiomics model: AUC = 0.912, 95% CI: 0.750-1.000; clinical model: AUC = 0.844, 95% CI: 0.578-1.000) and external validation set (nomogram: AUC = 0.971, 95% CI: 0.886-1.000; radiomics model: AUC = 0.928, 95% CI: 0.841-0.989; clinical model: AUC = 0.916,95% CI: 0.760-0.976). Conclusion All three models enable effective and non-invasive preoperative differentiation of benign from malignant SRMs, with the radiomics-clinical nomogram exhibiting the highest diagnostic accuracy, supporting its potential as a valuable clinical tool.

title: Preoperative respiratory muscle strength, muscle mass, and respiratory sarcopenia as predictors of postoperative pulmonary complications after thoracic and cardiac surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background & aims Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are common after thoracic, upper abdominal, and cardiac surgery and are associated with adverse outcomes. Respiratory sarcopenia (RS), characterized by coexisting reductions in respiratory muscle mass and strength, may represent a clinically relevant prognostic phenotype, but its prognostic value remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess whether low preoperative respiratory muscle mass, reduced strength, or their coexistence as RS or probable RS predicts PPCs after thoracic and cardiac surgery. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL from January 1990 to February 2026 for studies relating preoperative respiratory muscle mass, strength or flow, or RS to PPCs. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality In Prognosis Studies tool. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were pooled using random-effects models after harmonizing effect directions such that ORs >1 denoted higher risk. Results Sixteen studies were included; all involved thoracic or cardiac surgery, and none included an upper abdominal cohort. Cutoff-based respiratory muscle strength or flow impairment was associated with increased odds of PPCs (OR 2.25, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.50-3.37; I 2 = 51.2%), with the most consistent association observed for percent-predicted peak expiratory flow (PEF) (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.43-2.90; I 2 = 0%). Continuous PEF was associated with PPCs, whereas ultrasound-based diaphragm indices showed smaller, non-significant associations. RS or probable RS was associated with PPCs (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.33-3.26; I 2 = 0%). Conclusions Preoperative functional respiratory muscle impairment, particularly reduced PEF, and RS or probable RS were associated with PPCs. Given that the evidence was limited, heterogeneous, and predominantly derived from thoracic surgery, prospective confirmation is needed.

title: Respiratory Instability-driven Cardiac Dose Deviation in Postmastectomy Deep Inspiration Breath-hold Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (DIBH VMAT): Development and External Validation of a Respiratory-informed Predictive Framework.
abstract: Aims Deep inspiration breath-hold (DIBH) reduces cardiac exposure during left-sided breast radiotherapy; however, treatment-day cardiac dose may differ from the planned dose because of variations in respiratory reproducibility and anatomy. The aim of this study was to develop and validate a framework for predicting fraction-level cardiac dose variation using routinely acquired respiratory, anatomical, and dosimetric information. Materials and methods A retrospective cohort of 150 patients treated with postmastectomy DIBH VMAT (volumetric modulated arc therapy) was analyzed. Models were developed using a 30-patient development cohort with patient-wise-nested cross-validation, externally validated in 20 independent patients using cone-beam CT-derived synthetic CT dose recalculation, and applied to a 100-patient deployment cohort. Separate models predicted deviation from planned per-fraction mean heart dose (ΔMHD) and left anterior descending coronary artery dose (ΔLADCA D0.03 cc) using treatment-day real-time position management (RPM)--derived respiratory features, planning computed tomography (CT)-derived geometric variables, and plan-derived dosimetric parameters. SHAP-based analysis was performed to identify influential predictors. Results The final Gradient Boosting model for ΔMHD achieved an internal validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.541 ± 0.035 centigray (cGy) and coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.642 ± 0.069. The Ridge Regression model for left anterior descending coronary artery (ΔLADCA) achieved an MAE of 23.413 ± 1.617 cGy and R 2 of 0.413 ± 0.082. External validation demonstrated good agreement for ΔMHD (MAE 0.58 cGy, R 2 = 0.641), whereas ΔLADCA showed lower performance (MAE 24.14 cGy, R 2 = 0.435). Stability index and baseline drift were key predictors. Conclusion Treatment-day-respiratory characteristics combined with anatomical and dosimetric variables can estimate fraction-level cardiac dose variation during DIBH radiotherapy. The framework may support verification-based clinical review, with further validation required before implementation.

title: A frequency-driven method for retinal vessel segmentation.
abstract: Background and objective Retinal vessel segmentation is essential for diagnosing and monitoring ocular and systemic diseases. However, most existing deep learning methods operate predominantly in the spatial domain, limiting their ability to capture fine vessel structures and maintain topological continuity, especially for thin and low-contrast vessels. Existing frequency-aware approaches mostly rely on fixed transforms or simple feature concatenation, lacking task-adaptive spectral modeling. We developed a frequency-driven framework to address these limitations. Methods We implemented FRetinalNet, a frequency-driven encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder employs a Frequency Feature Tuning Block (FFTBlock) that parameterizes convolutional kernels in the spectral domain and adaptively modulates them with contextual cues via inverse FFT. Spatial and frequency features from parallel branches are fused using a Frequency Aware Fusion Block (FaFBlock) with cross-modality attention. The decoder includes dual-resolution branches for fine boundary recovery and global structural coherence, along with an auxiliary decoder for complementary supervision. Training proceeds in two stages: Stage 1 pretrains the encoder with original and Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform inputs using consistency loss; Stage 2 transfers weights and fine-tunes under supervised objectives. We evaluated on DRIVE, STARE, and OCTA-500 using Dice, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and AUC. Results FRetinalNet achieved the highest Dice scores on DRIVE (0.8578) and STARE (0.8696) compared with state-of-the-art methods. On OCTA-500, it obtained the best Dice for arteries (0.8864) and veins (0.9055) on the 6mm subset, and the best arterial (0.9169) and venous (0.9101) Dice on the 3mm subset. Ablation studies confirmed that two-stage training improves Dice from 0.8390 to 0.8578, and that all proposed components provide complementary benefits. Conclusions Explicit integration of learnable spectral parameterization and cross-domain feature fusion improves delineation of fine structures and topological continuity. The two-stage training pipeline provides robust frequency-aware initialization across fundus and OCTA modalities.

title: Intrinsic dimension for evaluating and analyzing neural networks for medical image segmentation.
abstract: Background and objective Evaluating medical image segmentation models typically relies on expert annotations, which are scarce, costly, and time-consuming to obtain. Intrinsic dimension (ID), defined as the minimal number of parameters required to describe high-dimensional data, has been shown to correlate with model generalization in classification tasks, but whether this relationship extends to segmentation remains unclear. Methods In this study, we systematically investigate ID as a label-free indicator for evaluating segmentation performance, including the generalization of standard segmentation models and the adaptability of promptable foundation models (i.e., SAM-based models). We also perform a layer-wise ID analysis to characterize variations in latent representation complexity. Furthermore, we propose a novel, computation- and memory-efficient strategy for ID calculation to broaden its applications. Results We reveal the following findings: 1) For standard segmentation, lower ID values of training-sample representations are consistently associated with better generalization performance on unseen test samples, as measured by DSC. 2) For promptable segmentation, test-data ID consistently reflects model adaptability to specific target data compared to entropy, a metric commonly believed to predict performance. 3) Layer-wise ID in segmentation follows an initially increasing and then decreasing pattern, similar to that in classification. Conclusions Our findings suggest the potential of ID as a label-free indicator for assessing the generalization and adaptability of segmentation models, thereby supporting model selection in label-scarce clinical settings.

title: VAE-based synthetic volume generation for trabecular bone microarchitecture.
abstract: Background and objective Micro computed tomography (microCT) enables detailed characterization of trabecular bone microarchitecture through quantitative morphological parameters. However, trabecular bone exhibits morphological variability across species, anatomical locations, bone types, and physiological or pathological conditions. Individual microCT datasets generally represent only a limited portion of this morphological variability, which may constrain the development and validation of quantitative descriptors, image-processing pipelines, and computational models. This study presents a Variational Autoencoder (VAE)-based framework for generating synthetic trabecular bone images, with the potential to support more comprehensive investigations of trabecular microarchitecture. Methods The VAE is trained on individual microCT slices and learns a three-dimensional latent space in which the ordered sequence of slices is mapped onto a continuous trajectory. Generating a synthetic volume reduces to i) defining a latent space trajectory and ii) decoding its points into 2D images ensuring inter-slice coherence without requiring any explicit 3D architecture. An interactive trajectory editor allows the user to manipulate, extend, or resample the latent path, providing full control over the morphology, length, and resolution of the synthetic volume. The reconstruction capability of the VAE was assessed by comparing the original microCT slices with their VAE-based reconstructions, and the original microCT-derived volume with the corresponding 3D volume obtained from the VAE-based reconstructed images, using 2D and 3D descriptors of trabecular microarchitecture. New sequences of synthetic images could be generated by modifying latent-space trajectories through the editor, thereby enabling the generation of multiple synthetic 3D volumes with controlled morphological variability. In this study, one such sequence was generated, and the corresponding 3D synthetic volume was characterized using microarchitectural parameters. The resulting values were then compared with those reported in the literature to assess the plausibility of the generated structure. Results Comparison of the morphological descriptors showed a high degree of similarity between the VAE-reconstructed and original microCT images. The corresponding 3D volumes also exhibited comparable morphological characteristics, indicating that the reconstruction process preserved the main structural features of the original microCT sample. Finally, the synthetic volume generated by synthetic VAE-based images exhibited microarchitectural parameter values comparable to those reported in the literature. Conclusion These results provide support for the ability of the proposed framework to generate synthetic trabecular microarchitectures with coherent structural features. Therefore, the framework can support data augmentation for deep-learning model training and more extensive investigations of trabecular microarchitecture. Future developments will focus on linking selected morphological descriptors to the three latent-space axes, thereby expanding the range of microarchitectural variability that can be generated and investigated.

title: Ultrasound-controlled therapeutics for bladder cancer: Mechanisms, recent advances, and future perspectives.
abstract: Bladder cancer remains a significant clinical challenge, characterised by a high recurrence rate and substantial healthcare costs. Although advances in surgery, systemic therapy, and intravesical treatment have improved clinical outcomes, treatment-related toxicity, therapeutic resistance, and the persistently poor prognosis of advanced disease highlight the need for more effective therapeutic strategies. Ultrasound-based micro/nanotherapeutics offer a promising approach that combines deep tissue penetration with high focal precision in a non-invasive, externally controllable manner. This review summarises recent advances in ultrasound-mediated therapeutic strategies for bladder cancer, including ultrasound-mediated drug and gene delivery, sonodynamic therapy (SDT), and high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) ablation. It describes how ultrasound, often in combination with microbubbles or nanobubbles, enhances the delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs and therapeutic genes through cavitation-induced permeabilisation of biological barriers. It then examines the mechanisms underlying SDT-induced reactive oxygen species generation and its integration with chemodynamic therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and imaging, alongside tumour microenvironment (TME) modulation strategies such as hypoxia relief and antioxidant depletion that augment SDT efficacy. Finally, it discusses HIFU ablation, including nanoparticle-assisted strategies that enhance tumour destruction through combined thermal and mechanical effects. The limitations of each modality and future directions for clinical translation, including standardisation of ultrasound devices and exposure parameters, optimisation of nanoplatform design, and integration of artificial intelligence-based predictive models, are also discussed.

title: SCOPE-Med: Structure-Preserving and Contour-Oriented Pseudo-Label Reconstruction for mixed-domain semi-supervised medical image segmentation.
abstract: Mixed-domain semi-supervised medical image segmentation aims to learn segmentation models from a small labeled set in one domain and abundant unlabeled data from multiple unknown domains. Its central challenge is to construct reliable pseudo-supervision under substantial domain shift. Existing methods commonly infer pseudo-label reliability from confidence or predictive uncertainty at the sample, model, or complete-mask level, implicitly assuming uniform reliability across each prediction. Coarse anatomical support can remain relatively stable, whereas local contours and fine details are more sensitive to appearance variation and boundary ambiguity. This uneven sensitivity makes a single trust decision inadequate, because it may either retain corrupted local details or discard useful structural information. To address this issue, this paper proposes SCOPE-Med, a Structure-preserving and Contour-Oriented Pseudo-label rEconstruction framework for mixed-domain semi-supervised medical image segmentation. SCOPE-Med organizes heterogeneous teacher predictions into coarse structural components and detail-sensitive residuals through Gaussian decomposition. The structural components retain spatially coherent region-level information, while the residuals preserve local variation that may contain both useful corrections and domain-induced noise. Predictive uncertainty then regulates local residual correction and suppresses unstable detail injection in ambiguous regions. An auxiliary boundary prediction head and contour-constrained objective provide complementary geometric supervision during student optimization. Through decomposition, regulation, and reconstruction, SCOPE-Med refines pseudo-supervision at the component level instead of assigning a single confidence score to an entire prediction. Experiments are conducted on two public two-dimensional binary segmentation benchmarks. Across overlap- and boundary-sensitive metrics, SCOPE-Med achieves strong average performance under the evaluated mixed-domain settings.
